title: Open Verifiable Trust Community (OpenVTC)
author: OpenVTC

title: chore(deps): take trust-tasks 0.9, vta-sdk 0.25 and did-git-sign 0.4.5
body:
**The last repo in the fleet still resolving `trust-tasks-rs` 0.6.5.**

It could not move until now: `did-git-sign` 0.4.4 required `vta-sdk ^0.24`, which required `trust-tasks-rs ^0.6`, so openvtc's graph was pinned by a dependency two repos away. VGI 0.4.5, published today, closes that.

## What moves

| requirement | from | to |
|---|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.6 | **0.9** |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.5 | **0.8** |
| `vta-sdk` | 0.24 | **0.25** |
| `vta-service` (**dev**-dependency) | 0.15 | **0.17** |

`did-git-sign`'s `"0.4.3"` caret already admitted 0.4.5; the lockfile carries it.

## The dev-dependency is why the shipped-graph check isn't enough

`cargo tree -d -e normal,build` was **clean** while `-e normal,build,dev` still showed two `vta-sdk` and two `trust-tasks-rs`.

`openvtc-core` dev-depends on `vta-service` for the in-process `MockVta` the bootstrap e2e runs against, and that pin was a line behind. Its own comment states the rule — *"track this with the vta-sdk major"* — and 0.17 is the line built against `vta-sdk` 0.25, as 0.15 was against 0.23. I extended that comment's version ledger rather than rewriting it.

## One source change, seven sites

`CreateKeyRequest` gained `internal` (VTI #995), so the literals in `state_handler/relationship_actions.rs` and `state_handler/setup_sequence/vta.rs` name it.

**`None` is deliberate.** Absent is today's behaviour; `Some(true)` mints a CSPRNG key that is never exported, excluded from backup, and **cannot be recovered from the mnemonic or otherwise**. That is not a property to acquire by filling in a compiler error.

## Nothing else broke — and that was by prior design

This workspace consumes `trust-task-error` documents and emits none, and it was already written version-agnostically: a `TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_PREFIX` constant plus `is_trust_task_error_type`'s `starts_with`, with a test asserting the match holds across versions.

The framework's move to `trust-task-error/0.5` therefore needs **no change here**. The `0.1`/`0.2` literals in that module are the test proving exactly that, and are left alone.

## Comments updated

Both `Cargo.toml` blocks now record this move rather than the last one, including a new note that the duplicate check must cover the **dev** graph — the failure above would have been missed by the shipped-graph check alone.

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace` — **710 pass, 0 fail**
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — no errors
- `cargo tree -d -e normal,build` **and** `-e normal,build,dev` — neither lists `trust-tasks-rs`, `trust-tasks-capability-client`, `vta-sdk`, `vta-service`, `vti-common` or `affinidi-tdk`

## `vta-sdk`

## [0.25.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-sdk-v0.24.0...vta-sdk-v0.25.0) — 2026-08-17 ### Added - **vta-keys**: Add non-extractable internal signing keys ([#995](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/995)) An ordinary VTA key is BIP-32 derived, so anyone holding the 24-word mnemonic can reconstruct it offline. That is what makes the VTA recoverable, and equally what makes "the operator cannot obtain this key" false — the second limb of what eIDAS calls sole control. An internal key is generated from the system CSPRNG, has no derivation path, and is never returned by any surface. The VTA acts only as a signing oracle for it. Deliberately not a flag on the imported-key path. That path wraps its secrets under a KEK derived from the master seed (derive_kek(seed, salt)), so a non-extractable flag on it would be decorative: the boundary it claims to enforce has already been walked around. Internal keys get their own keyspace, INTERNAL_KEYS, with no seed involvement at any point, and that keyspace is in EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP by design — a backup carrying it would be an export of keys the VTA promises never to export, and restoring it elsewhere would clone a signer. Refused for did:webvh log entries, enforced in code rather than left to guidance. WebVH is append-only and each entry is authorised by the update key the previous entry named; an unrecoverable update key means that if storage is lost the DID can never be updated again by anyone, permanently, and every integration pinned to it is stranded. Credentials can be re-issued, an append-only identity log cannot. Internal keys remain fine as a signing verificationMethod inside a published document, where loss costs the ability to produce new signatures rather than control of the identity. The export refusal is not a permission check — admin is not a bypass, because the value of the origin is that no caller holds this power. There are two refusals (an early return and an in-match arm); removing either leaves the other, and removing both does not compile, since the match over KeyOrigin becomes non-exhaustive. An export path cannot silently reopen. Operator surfaces carry the cost prominently: `pnm keys create --internal` prints what is lost and requires the operator to type a confirmation phrase rather than mash y, the response repeats the warning, and docs/02-vta/ internal-keys.md covers when to use one, what actually protects it (enclave measurement + KMS, not a mnemonic), and the two things that genuinely destroy it. - **vta-service**: Present ISO mdoc credentials over OID4VP ([#993](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/993)) * feat(vta-service)!: present ISO mdoc credentials over OID4VP Completes mdoc support. A VTA could receive, verify and store an mdoc; it could not present one. This is the last piece, and it needed three things the other formats do not. An OID4VP session on the query wire. An mdoc's holder binding is a DeviceAuth signature over an ISO 18013-7 SessionTranscript, whose handover is [clientId, responseUri, nonce, mdocGeneratedNonce]. Two of those exist only in an OID4VP exchange, so a verifier that wants an mdoc supplies them; QueryBody gains an optional oid4vp_session carrying OID4VP's own field names, so a verifier can copy them out of its authorization request unrenamed. Absent, an mdoc is not offered at all rather than offered unbound. A DeviceAuth over invented handover values verifies nowhere and, worse, looks bound. The gate lives in match_held so matchable and presentable stay the same set: a matched-but-unpresentable credential bails the entire vp_token, not just itself, taking every other credential the verifier legitimately asked for with it. A mutation removing the gate fails the test that pins this. Holder identity that is key-shaped. ConsentGrant.holder_did becomes HolderIdentity::{Subject, DeviceKey}: every other format names a subject DID, while an mdoc names a device key discovered at receive. Both resolve to a did:key because ConsentRecord::verify_proof binds the proof's verificationMethod to the data subject — the variant records provenance that would otherwise be silently lost, not a different kind of value. A P-256 consent receipt. The device key signs its own receipt under ecdsa-jcs-2019 (affinidi-data-integrity 0.7.10), where every other format uses eddsa-jcs-2022. Signing the receipt with some other key would break the verificationMethod binding above; that is why the cryptosuite was added upstream rather than worked around here. Presentation itself is not a present_single arm: an mdoc vp_token entry is base64url CBOR of a DeviceResponse, not a W3C VP object, so present_mdoc sits beside it. Selective disclosure is by omission — only the [namespace, element] paths the query asked for are included.

body:
### Added

- **vta-keys**: Add non-extractable internal signing keys ([#995](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/995))

An ordinary VTA key is BIP-32 derived, so anyone holding the 24-word mnemonic
  can reconstruct it offline. That is what makes the VTA recoverable, and equally
  what makes "the operator cannot obtain this key" false — the second limb of what
  eIDAS calls sole control.

  An internal key is generated from the system CSPRNG, has no derivation path, and
  is never returned by any surface. The VTA acts only as a signing oracle for it.

  Deliberately not a flag on the imported-key path. That path wraps its secrets
  under a KEK derived from the master seed (derive_kek(seed, salt)), so a
  non-extractable flag on it would be decorative: the boundary it claims to
  enforce has already been walked around. Internal keys get their own keyspace,
  INTERNAL_KEYS, with no seed involvement at any point, and that keyspace is in
  EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP by design — a backup carrying it would be an export of keys
  the VTA promises never to export, and restoring it elsewhere would clone a
  signer.

  guidance. WebVH is append-only and each entry is authorised by the update key
  the previous entry named; an unrecoverable update key means that if storage is
  lost the DID can never be updated again by anyone, permanently, and every
  integration pinned to it is stranded. Credentials can be re-issued, an
  append-only identity log cannot. Internal keys remain fine as a signing
  verificationMethod inside a published document, where loss costs the ability to
  produce new signatures rather than control of the identity.

  the value of the origin is that no caller holds this power. There are two
  refusals (an early return and an in-match arm); removing either leaves the other,
  and removing both does not compile, since the match over KeyOrigin becomes
  non-exhaustive. An export path cannot silently reopen.

  prints what is lost and requires the operator to type a confirmation phrase
  rather than mash y, the response repeats the warning, and docs/02-vta/
  internal-keys.md covers when to use one, what actually protects it (enclave

An ordinary VTA key is BIP-32 derived, so anyone holding the 24-word mnemonic
  can reconstruct it offline. That is what makes the VTA recoverable, and equally
  what makes "the operator cannot obtain this key" false — the second limb of what
  eIDAS calls sole control.

  An internal key is generated from the system CSPRNG, has no derivation path, and
  is never returned by any surface. The VTA acts only as a signing oracle for it.

  Deliberately not a flag on the imported-key path. That path wraps its secrets
  under a KEK derived from the master seed (derive_kek(seed, salt)), so a
  non-extractable flag on it would be decorative: the boundary it claims to
  enforce has already been walked around. Internal keys get their own keyspace,
  INTERNAL_KEYS, with no seed involvement at any point, and that keyspace is in
  EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP by design — a backup carrying it would be an export of keys
  the VTA promises never to export, and restoring it elsewhere would clone a
  signer.

  Refused for did:webvh log entries, enforced in code rather than left to
  guidance. WebVH is append-only and each entry is authorised by the update key
  the previous entry named; an unrecoverable update key means that if storage is
  lost the DID can never be updated again by anyone, permanently, and every
  integration pinned to it is stranded. Credentials can be re-issued, an
  append-only identity log cannot. Internal keys remain fine as a signing
  verificationMethod inside a published document, where loss costs the ability to
  produce new signatures rather than control of the identity.

  The export refusal is not a permission check — admin is not a bypass, because
  the value of the origin is that no caller holds this power. There are two
  refusals (an early return and an in-match arm); removing either leaves the other,
  and removing both does not compile, since the match over KeyOrigin becomes
  non-exhaustive. An export path cannot silently reopen.

  Operator surfaces carry the cost prominently: `pnm keys create --internal`
  prints what is lost and requires the operator to type a confirmation phrase
  rather than mash y, the response repeats the warning, and docs/02-vta/
  internal-keys.md covers when to use one, what actually protects it (enclave
  measurement + KMS, not a mnemonic), and the two things that genuinely destroy
  it.

- **vta-service**: Present ISO mdoc credentials over OID4VP ([#993](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/993))

* feat(vta-service)!: present ISO mdoc credentials over OID4VP

  Completes mdoc support. A VTA could receive, verify and store an mdoc; it could
  not present one. This is the last piece, and it needed three things the other
  formats do not.

  An OID4VP session on the query wire. An mdoc's holder binding is a DeviceAuth
  signature over an ISO 18013-7 SessionTranscript, whose handover is
  [clientId, responseUri, nonce, mdocGeneratedNonce]. Two of those exist only in
  an OID4VP exchange, so a verifier that wants an mdoc supplies them; QueryBody
  gains an optional oid4vp_session carrying OID4VP's own field names, so a
  verifier can copy them out of its authorization request unrenamed.

  Absent, an mdoc is not offered at all rather than offered unbound. A DeviceAuth
  over invented handover values verifies nowhere and, worse, looks bound. The gate
  lives in match_held so matchable and presentable stay the same set: a
  matched-but-unpresentable credential bails the entire vp_token, not just itself,
  taking every other credential the verifier legitimately asked for with it. A
  mutation removing the gate fails the test that pins this.

  Holder identity that is key-shaped. ConsentGrant.holder_did becomes
  HolderIdentity::{Subject, DeviceKey}: every other format names a subject DID,
  while an mdoc names a device key discovered at receive. Both resolve to a
  did:key because ConsentRecord::verify_proof binds the proof's
  verificationMethod to the data subject — the variant records provenance that
  would otherwise be silently lost, not a different kind of value.

  A P-256 consent receipt. The device key signs its own receipt under
  ecdsa-jcs-2019 (affinidi-data-integrity 0.7.10), where every other format uses
  eddsa-jcs-2022. Signing the receipt with some other key would break the
  verificationMethod binding above; that is why the cryptosuite was added upstream
  rather than worked around here.

  Presentation itself is not a present_single arm: an mdoc vp_token entry is
  base64url CBOR of a DeviceResponse, not a W3C VP object, so present_mdoc sits
  beside it. Selective disclosure is by omission — only the [namespace, element]
  paths the query asked for are included.

title: chore(deps)!: track trust-tasks 0.9 across the workspace
body:
## What

Moves all five `trust-tasks-*` requirements plus `trust-tasks-capability-client` (0.5 → 0.8) together, and takes the `affinidi-messaging-*` releases built on 0.9 alongside them.

| dependency | from | to |
|---|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.6 | **0.9** |
| `trust-tasks-https` | 0.6 | **0.9** |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm` | 0.6 | **0.9** |
| `trust-tasks-proof` | 0.6 | **0.9** |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.5 | **0.8** |
| `affinidi-messaging-sdk` (transitive) | 0.19.7 | 0.19.8 |
| `affinidi-messaging-mediator` (transitive) | 0.18.17 | 0.18.18 |

They move as one because `trust-tasks-rs`'s core types cross the public API of `-https` / `-didcomm` / `-proof` — a graph mixing majors does not type-check.

## What cost nothing

- **No `consume_inbound` call sites in this workspace**, so 0.9.0's new required `PayloadPolicy` argument does not reach us.
- **Nothing matches on `StandardCode`**, so 0.7.0's `#[non_exhaustive]` does not either.
- The `validate` feature stays enabled and unused, exactly as before.

## What did change: the error version on the wire

`trust-task-error` moved 0.3 → 0.4 → 0.5 upstream. Each step happened for the same reason the 0.3 step did — a new standard code the older payload schema's `code` enum does not list and whose extended-code pattern does not match, so a document carrying it would not validate as the older version. `0.4` carries `idConflict`, `0.5` carries `cancelled` (SPEC §8.3).

Both services hand-write that version on their **one unrouted path** — where there is no request document to reject from, and therefore no framework call to ask. Both were left naming `0.3` while `reject_with` stamped `0.5` on every *routed* rejection. One service emitting two versions is a trap for exactly the consumer that pins one of them.

**`unrouted_and_routed_errors_agree_on_the_type_uri` exists in both services to catch this, and it did.** The bump failed those two tests rather than shipping two dialects. That is the test doing its job; constants updated and their rationale extended.

## Fixture tidy-up (and why the census count was not raised)

Two in-`src` VTC test fixtures also named `0.3`. They now take the version from `framework_error_type_uri()` rather than repeating it, so they follow the emitter on the next bump instead of stranding a version behind.

That also keeps `trust_task_manifest`'s unpublished-URI census at **one** URI for the family. The census is deliberately exact so the debt can shrink but never grow unnoticed, and its own failure message says raising the expected count is the wrong fix — so I didn't.

**Backward acceptance of an older error document keeps its coverage:** `vtc-service/tests/registry_didcomm.rs` pins `0.1` on purpose and is left alone.

## Compatibility

Per SPEC §5.2 forward-minor compatibility, a consumer still pinned to `trust-task-error/0.3` SHOULD accept `0.5`. Marked `!` because this changes the version on the wire, not because any Rust signature moved.

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace` — all suites pass, 0 failures
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo tree -d -e normal,build` lists **none** of `trust-tasks-rs`, `trust-tasks-capability-client`, `vta-sdk`, `vti-common`, `affinidi-tdk`
- `scripts/check-lockfile-self-pins.sh` — no self-pin
- **No `version =` field touched**, per RELEASING.md — versions are the Release PR's job

### Unrelated pre-existing breakage found while verifying

`cargo check --workspace --all-features --all-targets` fails in `vta-sdk/tests/provision_client_e2e.rs` (5 × `E0609`). **Not caused by this PR** — it reproduces on `main`. PR #949 (`fix(provisioning)!: relay the holder's bootstrap VP as raw JSON`) changed `ProvisionIntegrationRequest::request` to `serde_json::Value` on 2026-08-12 without updating that test, and no CI job builds `--all-features --all-targets`, so it went unnoticed. Left for a separate fix; flagging it here rather than folding it in.

title: feat(join): explicit paste row; remove 13 unreachable setup pages
body:
The two follow-ups flagged when [vti-setup#29](https://github.com/OpenVTC/vti-setup/issues/29) and [vti-setup#31](https://github.com/OpenVTC/vti-setup/issues/31) were closed by #227.

## 1. An explicit `[Ctrl+V]` paste action on the join entry page

#29 was filed as *"I cannot find anywhere to paste/import the VIC"*. #227 raised the tip's contrast and moved it above the input, which treats the symptom — bracketed paste worked the whole time, but an affordance nobody can see is not an affordance.

`Action::JoinPasteFromClipboard` reads the OS clipboard and runs it through the same `load_pasted_vic` validation as a bracketed paste, and the key is named on screen in every invitation state:

```
  Have an invitation?
  Load the invitation credential (VIC) JSON — it fills in the community DID
  for you and rides along with the join request.
  [Ctrl+V] paste an invitation from the clipboard, or paste the JSON straight in
```

Ctrl+V is intercepted ahead of the `tui_input` fallthrough so it loads a credential rather than typing a `v` into the DID field; a bare `v` still types. Rows fall back to a short form on narrow terminals rather than clipping. Reading the clipboard is arboard-only and fails over SSH by design, so the failure message points back at bracketed paste, which works everywhere.

## 2. Removing the unreachable setup pages

#31's scope grew once I traced reachability properly from `StartAsk`. Nothing navigates to `MediatorAsk` **or** `WebvhServerSelect`, and every other orphan hangs off one of those two:

| Orphan root | Reachable only from |
|---|---|
| `MediatorAsk` | — nothing |
| `MediatorCustom`, `UserName` | `MediatorAsk` |
| `WebVHAddress` | `UserName` |
| `WebvhServerSelect` | — nothing |
| `WebvhServerProgress`, `VtaKeysFetch` | `WebvhServerSelect` |
| `DIDKeysShow` | `VtaKeysFetch` / `WebvhServerProgress` (or `Action::SetDIDKeys`, never sent) |
| `DidKeysExportAsk/Inputs/Show`, `DidGitSignAsk`, `DidGitSignSetup` | `DIDKeysShow` |

Thirteen pages, ~3,800 lines. Also removed: ten `Action` variants, sixteen `SetupEvent` variants, four `SetupState` sub-structs (`DidGitSignSetupState`, `DIDKeysExportState`, `WebvhServerState`, plus `WebVHAddress`'s progress fields), `vta.use_webvh_server` / `vta.webvh_servers`, and the webvh-server probe provisioning ran on every setup to fill a list nothing read.

**What deliberately stays.** `SetupState` keeps the fields those pages *wrote* — `did_keys`, `webvh_address`, `custom_mediator`, `username`. The join flow (`join_flow.rs:1016`) and the standalone persona mint (`create_persona.rs:89`) fill the same struct themselves before calling `Config::mint_persona_into`, so deleting them would have broken minting outright. Only the members no live writer touches are gone.

Since the persona pages are gone rather than dormant, the setup header collapses further than in #227: the `use_webvh_server` branch and its alternate "DID & Keys / Display Name" labels go too, leaving one four-step list.

## One thing worth deciding separately

Installing did-git-sign was only ever offered by `DidGitSignAsk`, so **it has been unreachable since R-A-5 regardless of this PR** — this deletes code that already could not run. The main page still *detects* an existing did-git-sign config (`detect_did_git_sign_info`), so that panel shows nothing with no in-app way to fix it. Re-offering the install needs a new entry point, which is a product decision rather than a cleanup. Same story, less sharply, for PGP key export.

## Testing

`cargo test --workspace` green, clippy clean, and checked under **both** feature configurations — the openpgp-card token pages read `setup.did_keys` and are still reachable through the protection sub-flow, so a `--features openpgp-card` build was the thing most likely to break on this deletion.

New tests: Ctrl+V routes to `JoinPasteFromClipboard` without reaching the input, a bare `v` still types, and the paste key is drawn in all three invitation states at two widths. Fifteen navigation tests covering the deleted events went with them.

title: feat(vta-keys)!: add non-extractable internal signing keys
body:
## Why

An ordinary VTA key is BIP-32 derived, so **anyone holding the 24-word mnemonic
can reconstruct it offline**. That is what makes the VTA recoverable — and
equally what makes *"the operator cannot obtain this key"* false, which is the
second limb of what eIDAS calls **sole control**.

An internal key is generated from the system CSPRNG, has no derivation path, and
is never returned by any surface. The VTA acts only as a signing oracle for it.

## The detail that decides whether this works

**It is deliberately not a flag on the imported-key path.** That path wraps
secrets under a KEK derived from the master seed (`derive_kek(seed, salt)`), so a
"non-extractable" flag on it would be decorative — the boundary it claims to
enforce has already been walked around, and the mnemonic still reconstructs the
key.

So internal keys get their own keyspace, `INTERNAL_KEYS`, with **no seed
involvement at any point**, and that keyspace is in `EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP` by
design rather than omission. A backup carrying it would be an export of keys the
VTA promises never to export, and restoring one elsewhere would silently clone a
signer.

## Refused for `did:webvh`, enforced in code

WebVH is append-only: each entry is authorised by the update key the previous
entry named. If an unrecoverable key were the update key and storage were lost,
the DID could **never be updated again by anyone**, permanently, and every
integration pinned to it would be stranded.

The distinction isn't "how important is this key" — it's **"if it vanishes, is
there a path back?"** Credentials can be re-issued. An append-only identity log
cannot. So the refusal lives in `did_webvh`, not in a doc note.

Internal keys remain fine as a **signing `verificationMethod`** in a published
document, where loss costs the ability to produce new signatures rather than
control of the identity.

## The export refusal is not a permission check

Admin is not a bypass, because the value of the origin is that *no* caller holds
this power — treating it as an authorization question would be the wrong shape.

There are two refusals: an early return and an in-match arm. I mutation-tested
both:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| remove the early return | in-match arm still refuses ✓ |
| remove **both** | **does not compile** — the `KeyOrigin` match becomes non-exhaustive ✓ |

That second row is the stronger guarantee: an export path cannot silently reopen,
because the type system stops you. The tests pin the *message*; exhaustiveness
pins the *existence*.

## Operator surfaces carry the cost

`pnm keys create --internal` prints exactly what is lost — mnemonic won't recover
it, excluded from backup, never exported, storage loss is permanent, and the
webvh restriction — then requires the operator to **type a confirmation phrase**
rather than mash `y`. A habitual yes/no prompt isn't proportionate to a
permanent, silent loss of signing ability. `--yes` exists for automation.

The response repeats the warning (and `CreateKeyResponse` gained `origin`, so an
API consumer sees it too). `docs/02-vta/internal-keys.md` covers when to use one,
what actually protects it — **enclave measurement + KMS, not a mnemonic** — and
the two things that genuinely destroy it: losing the KMS key, or losing sealed
storage without a replica.

It's also explicit that in **non-TEE** deployments this is meaningful hygiene
against export, not a tamper-proofing claim: an operator with disk access is
inside that boundary.

## Enforcement summary

| Surface | Internal key |
|---|---|
| `keys/sign` | **Allowed** — the only use |
| Key export | **Refused**, including super-admin |
| Internal-authority export | **Refused** |
| `backup export` | **Excluded** (keyspace not backed up) |
| `did:webvh` log signing | **Refused** |
| DID document `verificationMethod` | **Allowed** |

## Breaking changes

All 0.x; release-plz moves the compatibility fields.

- `KeyOrigin` gains `Internal`
- `CreateKeyParams` gains `internal`; wire `CreateKeyBody` / `CreateKeyRequest`
  gain an optional `internal`
- `CreateKeyResponse` gains `origin`
- `create_key` and `sign_payload` take the internal keyspace

## Testing

**3225 workspace tests pass**, `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` and
`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` clean (one pre-existing `backup_export`
deprecation in the e2e tests, untouched by this change).

New: 6 in `vta-keys::internal` (signature verifies under the advertised public
key; keys are independent; overwrite refused; delete is final; X25519 refused)
and 4 in `operations::keys` (no export even for super-admin; internal authority
doesn't bypass; signing works; explicit key id required).

title: fix(ux): prefill the community from a pasted VIC; drop the phantom setup step
body:
Fixes the three UX defects reported in [OpenVTC/vti-setup#29](https://github.com/OpenVTC/vti-setup/issues/29) and [OpenVTC/vti-setup#31](https://github.com/OpenVTC/vti-setup/issues/31). Grouped into one PR because they are all the same surface — what the operator sees on the way into a community.

## 1. A pasted VIC now fills in the community it is for (#29)

> Pressing Enter at this point does nothing. You still have to copy/paste in the VTC DID as well to continue.

Two bugs behind that one sentence.

**Enter was a silent no-op.** `VtcEnterDid::handle_key_event` only sent `JoinSubmitVtc` when the trimmed input was non-empty — otherwise the keypress vanished with no message, no error, nothing. A paste routes to `Action::JoinPasteVic` and never touches `vtc_did`, so after pasting an invitation the field is still empty and the page looks frozen. Enter now submits unconditionally and the handler answers an empty field with a reason on screen.

**The DID was already in hand.** A VIC's issuer *is* the community's VTC DID — `openvtc_core::join::invitation_issuer` says so outright, and `validate_invitation_credential` already requires the issuer to be extractable before a paste is accepted. Nothing read it: `invitation_issuer` had no callers in the TUI crate. The entry-page paste now records it, and the component prefills the input from it.

**Prefilled, not auto-submitted.** An invitation is handed to you by someone else, so the community it points at stays visible and editable before Enter commits to joining it. The loaded-invitation line now names that community, which is what makes the prefill checkable rather than magic.

The prefill is guarded so it never fights the operator: `move_with_state` runs on every state broadcast, so a `prefilled_issuer` field records what was last stamped in. A DID typed by hand survives a paste, an edited prefill survives every later redraw, and a paste re-arms the guard so clearing the field and pasting the same VIC again fills it back in.

## 2. The invitation prompt is legible and sits where it is needed (#29)

> note the hard-to-see "Tip: paste an invitation credential (VIC) here to auto-join"

It was `COLOR_DARK_GRAY` italic — deliberately the dimmest text on the page — rendered *below* the input, below the orange examples block, and below any errors. The least important content on the screen was the loudest.

The invitation status and any error now sit directly above the input in full-contrast colours, and the tip leads with a bold **Have an invitation?** rather than a dim "Tip:". Everything in that block is wrapped to the terminal width instead of clipping its tail — reusing `wrap_text`, which already hard-splits DIDs and JSON. The block is sized by line count and clamped so a terminal too short for it clips prose rather than the input field.

Worth noting for the record: as *filed*, #29 was a discoverability report — the reporter could not find anywhere to import a VIC at all. Raising the contrast and moving it above the fold is the fix here; if that is still not enough, the next step is an explicit paste row like the one `InvitationChoice` already carries.

## 3. Setup no longer advertises a step it will never run (#31)

R-A-5 ended setup at profile security (`UnlockCode*` → `FinalPage`); a persona is minted later by the State-B join flow. The persona pages are already marked `#[allow(dead_code)]` with a comment saying exactly that, and nothing anywhere navigates to `SetupPage::MediatorAsk`.

But `render_setup_header` still hardcoded `total_step = 5` and an `is_identity` group that could never match — so the wizard went 3/5 → 5/5 with an unticked "Digital Identity" in between, which is what the reporter saw. Both label lists drop to four steps: the `use_webvh_server` branch's "Display Name" (`UserName`) is reachable only via `UseDefaultMediator` from the same dead `MediatorAsk`, so it was equally stranded.

## Testing

`cargo test --workspace` green, clippy clean. New coverage:

- **Issuer capture** — string and object `issuer` forms both yield the community DID, and a rejected paste (bad JSON, not a VIC) leaves no issuer behind. That last one matters: an issuer surviving a refused paste would prefill a community DID from a credential that will not be presented.
- **Prefill guards** — fills an empty field; leaves an edited prefill alone on redraw; a typed DID survives a paste; clearing the invitation and re-pasting both re-arm it.
- **Render tests** — draw the page to a `TestBackend` and read the buffer back: the paste affordance precedes both the input and the examples, a loaded invitation names its community, the input stays directly under its prompt across all four states at three widths, and a 40×14 terminal still shows the input.

The render tests are the ones that earn their keep — the header is sized by line count, so a line that wrapped where it was assumed not to would silently push the input off its row.

title: consumeInbound never validates payload schemas — REQUIRED members are unenforced
body:
Found re-proving the witnessed exchange on published 0.7.0 ([ref-06w4](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06w4-package-truth), each case a named check). The generated spec objects expose only `{ typeUri, isBearer, isProofRequired, isRecipientRequired }` — no schema — so the §7.2 schema step never runs: a `vrc/relationships/propose` with a nonsense payload is handled, and responses missing REQUIRED `vwcDigestMultibase` / `vrcDigestMultibase` (the #213 correlators) are accepted. Policy checks (proof, recipient, error routing) all work; only payload-schema validation is absent. The schemas ship in the package as TypeScript types and `payload.schema.json` files, which impose nothing at runtime.

Untested whether `trust-tasks-rs` shares this.

Minor, same area: a handler returning `undefined` crashes `consumeInbound` with a bare TypeError (`isErrorResponse` reads `.type` unguarded) — treating that as handled-no-reply would fit fire-and-forget consumers.

**TL;DR: the TS runtime enforces proof rules but not schemas, so every REQUIRED payload member is optional in practice. Happy to take the fix as a PR — wire the shipped schemas into the spec objects and validate in `consumeInbound`.**

title: feat(vta-service)!: present ISO mdoc credentials over OID4VP
body:
## Why

A VTA could receive, verify and store an mdoc. It could not **present** one.
This is the last piece — and it needed three things no other format does.

## 1. An OID4VP session on the query wire

An mdoc's holder binding is a `DeviceAuth` signature over an ISO 18013-7
`SessionTranscript`, whose handover is
`[clientId, responseUri, nonce, mdocGeneratedNonce]`. **Two of those exist only
in an OID4VP exchange** — a Trust-Task envelope has no `response_uri`.

So `QueryBody` gains an optional `oid4vp_session`, carrying OID4VP's own field
names (not this workspace's camelCase) so a verifier copies them straight out of
its authorization request.

**Absent, an mdoc is not offered at all** — not offered unbound. A `DeviceAuth`
over invented handover values verifies nowhere and, worse, *looks* like holder
binding.

The gate lives in `match_held`, not in the present path, so **matchable and
presentable stay the same set**. A matched-but-unpresentable credential bails
the *entire* `vp_token`, taking every other credential the verifier legitimately
asked for. Mutation-checked: removing the gate fails
`an_mdoc_does_not_match_without_an_oid4vp_session`.

## 2. Holder identity that is key-shaped

`ConsentGrant.holder_did` → `HolderIdentity::{Subject, DeviceKey}`.

Every other format names a subject DID. An mdoc names a **device key**,
discovered at receive (#990). Both variants still resolve to a `did:key`,
because `ConsentRecord::verify_proof` binds the proof's `verificationMethod` to
the data subject — a bare key id there would make every receipt unverifiable.
The variant records provenance that would otherwise be silently lost, rather
than a different kind of value.

## 3. A P-256 consent receipt

The device key signs its own receipt under **`ecdsa-jcs-2019`**
([affinidi-data-integrity 0.7.10](https://github.com/affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs/pull/713)),
where every other format uses `eddsa-jcs-2022`.

This is why that suite was added upstream rather than worked around: signing the
receipt with *some other* key would break the `verificationMethod` binding
above, and there was no ECDSA Data Integrity suite in the stack at all.

## Presentation shape

`present_mdoc` sits **beside** `present_single`, not inside it — an mdoc
`vp_token` entry is base64url CBOR of a `DeviceResponse`, not a W3C VP object.
Selective disclosure is by omission: only the `[namespace, element]` paths the
query asked for are included.

## Breaking changes

At 0.x, and release-plz moves the compatibility fields:

- `ConsentGrant.holder_did` → `ConsentGrant.holder`
- `match_vault` takes the session; `match_held` takes `can_bind_mdoc`
- `QueryBody` gains a field

## Testing

`vta-service` **819 passed**, `vta-vault` 104 passed. fmt + clippy clean, zero
warnings across `--all-targets`.

New tests:
- **the gate**, both directions — an mdoc must not match without a session, *and
  must* match with one (otherwise the gate is just breaking mdoc support)
- **candidate shape** — claims keyed by namespace, not flat, plus `doctype`
  populated. DCQL addresses mdoc claims as `[namespace, elementIdentifier]`; a
  flat tree matches nothing and the failure reads as "the holder doesn't have
  it"

Mutation-checked: removing the session gate fails the gate test.

## Where this leaves mdoc

Receive → verify against configured IACA roots → refuse an unpresentable one →
match by doctype → present with holder binding. Both eIDAS-mandated credential
formats are now supported end to end.

title: fix(libs): consumeInbound performs §7.2 item 2, and says so when it does not
body:
Closes #230. Reported by @albertoleon7794, whose proposed fix — "wire the shipped schemas into the spec objects and validate in `consumeInbound`" — is what this does. ## The defect, and a correction to its framing `consume.ts` documented items 1, 2 and 3 as out of scope: *"they belong to the caller's parse and dispatch, and by the time you hold a typed document they have already succeeded."* For item 2 that was never true in TypeScript. `TrustTaskDocument

` is a compile-time type that erases to nothing, so a `JSON.parse` result cast to it has been checked by nobody. Worse, the package shipped **no schema a caller could have validated against** — `SPEC` carried four booleans, and the `payload.schema.json` files weren't reachable as values. The step was delegated to a caller with no way to perform it. Reproduced before touching anything — a `witness/session/submit` `#response` with `payload: {total: "nonsense"}`, missing *both* REQUIRED members: ``` A: payload missing every REQUIRED member -> handled B: handler returned undefined -> THREW TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'type') ``` **On the issue's open question — `trust-tasks-rs` does *not* share this.** Probed rather than assumed, on the same spec: | case | Rust | |---|---| | missing REQUIRED member | rejected | | `DigestMultibase` `minLength`/`pattern` violated | rejected (validating newtype) | | `additionalProperties: false` violated | rejected (unknown field) | | `ext` `propertyNames` pattern violated | rejected | | **`ext` `minProperties: 1` violated** | **accepted** ← the residue | serde and typify perform most of item 2 at deserialization. What survives is what a Rust type cannot express — `minProperties`, `minItems` on an optional array, conditional subschemas — which `trust-tasks-rs` had the machinery to catch (`ValidatedPayload`, `schema_index::schema_for`) and never called from `consume_inbound`. So the two libraries were failing *differently*: TypeScript enforced nothing, Rust enforced most things quietly. `consume.ts` exists to keep the two reaching the same verdict, so both are fixed together. ## The fix Both take a payload policy as a **required** argument, mirroring the existing proof policy: ```ts await consumeInbound({ spec: AclGrant_v0_1.SPEC, proofPolicy: { kind: "verify", verify: myVerifier }, payloadPolicy: { kind: "validate", validate: myValidator }, // or "acceptUnvalidated" // … }); ``` ```rust consume_inbound( transport, ProofPolicy::Verify(&verifier), PayloadPolicy::Validate(&validator), // or PayloadPolicy::::AcceptUnvalidated doc, my_vid, now, error_id, handler, ).await ``` Neither library bundles a JSON Schema engine, for the reason neither bundles a cryptosuite: the engine, its draft support and its resource limits belong to the consumer, and the npm package stays dependency-free. What they now ship is the **schema** — the part a caller cannot reconstruct. Required rather than defaulted because a default of "skip" preserves exactly the reported defect for everyone who doesn't go looking. The Rust docs are explicit that its `Validate` buys less than the name suggests, so nobody picks the opt-out believing it costs nothing. **Response variants carry a schema for the first time** — only request payloads had one, and the reported defect was found on a response. ## Two independent `$ref` inliners, held to each other The shipped schemas are self-contained: cross-file `$ref`s into `_shared/` and `_framework/` are inlined so a runtime validator needs no resolver. That means two implementations of the same splice — `resolve_cross_file_refs` (Rust) and `inlineCrossFileRefs` (TS). `npm run check-bindings` now asserts they produce the **same document** (key-sorted compare, so formatting differences aren't failures) and that neither leaves an external `$ref` behind. Per CLAUDE.md's warning about DRYing this file up, it does *not* re-derive the expected schema — it holds the two generators to each other, which is the property neither can establish alone. Verified non-vacuous by perturbing one side: ``` - acl/grant/0.1: the request schema shipped by trust-tasks-ts and the one shipped by trust-tasks-rs are not the same document. The two $ref inliners have diverged, so the two libraries would disagree about which payloads conform. ``` ## The crash, and the gap behind it A handler returning nothing hit `isErrorResponse` reading `.type` unguarded. The real problem was that there was **no way to express "handled, no reply"** — SPEC §4.4.1 specifically contemplates a specification with no success response, whose consumers MUST NOT emit one, and the handler's return type demanded a document or an error. New `accepted` outcome; the handler may return void. A JavaScript caller who omits the new required option gets a message naming it, not a property-read failure — checked in the smoke test, since JS callers get no compile-time signal. ## Breaking — 0.9.0 on both libraries - `consume_inbound` gains a third positional argument and a seventh generic parameter. `NoValidator` pins that parameter on the `AcceptUnvalidated` path, which carries no validator to infer from. - `ValidatedPayload::SCHEMA_JSON` is gone. The schema is now `Payload::PAYLOAD_SCHEMA: Option<&'static str>`, emitted **unconditionally** rather than behind the `validate` feature — it's a `&'static str` and costs no dependency, and gating it was precisely what kept the schema out of reach. `ValidatedPayload` becomes a blanket impl over every `Payload`, replacing ~300 generated impl blocks. - `schema_index::schema_for` is likewise no longer feature-gated. - `ConsumeOutcome` gains a variant, so exhaustive switches need a new arm. Per CLAUDE.md's workspace-event rule, the six crates pinning `trust-tasks-rs = "0.8"` move to `"0.9"` and release with it: `-https` / `-didcomm` / `-proof` / `-tsp` → 0.9.0, `-capability-client` → 0.8.0, `-didcomm-v1` → 0.7.0. ## Verification `npm run validate` (306 specs) · `npm run check-bindings` (306 TS / 301 Rust, incl. the new schema cross-check) · `cargo test --workspace` **493 passed, 0 failed** · `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate` · `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` clean · `cargo fmt --check` clean · `npm test` in `trust-tasks-ts` **50 passed** (11 new) · `npm run smoke` · `npm run test:infra`. New tests assert the things that would otherwise pass vacuously: that the validator is **consulted at all**, that it runs **before the handler**, that a *throwing* validator is a rejection rather than a pass, that `acceptUnvalidated` genuinely skips, and that generated `SPEC`/`RESPONSE_SPEC` carry inlined schemas. ## Note for reviewers The diff is 631 files, but only ~10 are hand-written — the rest is regenerated bindings carrying their new `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA` constant. Worth reviewing: `trust-tasks-rs/src/consume.rs`, `src/payload.rs`, `src/validate.rs`, `trust-tasks-ts/src/_runtime/consume.ts`, `scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs`, `scripts/check-bindings-conformance.mjs`.

title: fix(specs): the taskContext id locates the session document; a digest binds it
body:
## The problem, plainly

A Verifiable Witness Credential points back at the witness session it came from with `taskContext` — which today is just the session document's **id**. An id is a name, not evidence. Anyone can write a *different* session document — different parties, different content — and give it the same id. A verifier that pairs the credential with a session document by comparing ids will accept that counterfeit, and the credential now appears to attest a ceremony that never happened that way.

This came out of a DTG Core Credentials sync: "nothing stops me creating a different trust task with the same document ID — it's not proof of anything." Two candidate fixes were named there: anchor on the document's **proof value**, or on a **hash of the whole document**. We built both and attacked both before proposing anything.

## What we tried, and what happened

The trial is running code: [ref-06w3-taskcontext-binding](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06w3-taskcontext-binding) — one forged `witness/session` document carrying a genuine id, paired against the same VWC under each rule. 13 checks.

| Binding rule | Genuine document | Forged document (same id) | Unproofed document |
|---|---|---|---|
| **id only** (the specs today) | pairs | **pairs — the forgery is accepted** | pairs |
| **digest** of the whole document | pairs | **rejected** — her content hashes to a different value | **works** — no proof needed |
| **proofValue, compared as a string** | pairs | **fooled** — she copies the genuine proof block verbatim, and the strings match | **impossible — an unproofed document has no proofValue** |
| **proofValue, with full signature verification** | pairs | rejected | impossible |

Three things decided it:

1. **The digest catches the forgery unconditionally.** The check *recomputes* the value from the document in front of the verifier — wrong content mathematically cannot produce the right value. There is nothing to copy.
2. **proofValue only binds if you verify the signature** — the string alone can be pasted onto a counterfeit. And full signature verification (canonicalize + hash + resolve the signer's key + verify) costs *more* than the digest check (canonicalize + hash, measured at ~5 µs).
3. **proofValue sometimes doesn't exist.** `witness/session` 0.1 declares `proofRequirement.request: OPTIONAL` — and the session request *is* the document `taskContext` points at. A conforming unproofed session has nothing to anchor to.

So: **the id stays as the locator** (cheap lookup, conformant with SPEC §4.9.1), and the credential gains **`taskDigestMultibase`** as the binder — a digest over the session document's JCS (RFC 8785) canonical form *excluding `proof`* (so signed and unsigned forms of the same document hash identically), in the registry's `DigestMultibase` encoding. Where a proof exists, its proofValue remains a fine index key; it is not the binding.

## What this PR changes

The credential's schema belongs to DTG Core Credentials and is amended there (staged into trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#18). This PR is the small companion on the witness specs, whose pairing checklist currently teaches the id-only comparison:

- **`witness/session/submit` spec** — the MUST-clause extends from "taskContext MUST equal the id" to "…and taskDigestMultibase MUST reproduce over that document"; the holder ships the session document alongside the retained `#response`; the verifier's pairing checklist gains the digest-match step.
- **`witness/session/submit` payload schema** — the `vwc` member's description states the same rule.
- **`witness/session` spec** — the paragraph that introduces the anchor names the locator/binder split.

No wire-shape change to any published payload (`vwc` is opaque here) — descriptive text and prose only. Bindings regenerated (Rust + TS) and both libraries bumped in lockstep to 0.7.1 per CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md. If the in-place amendment fights the versioning rules, happy to re-cut as 0.2s.

title: feat(framework): a citation carries a task digest, not just an id (§4.9.3)
body:
Carries [#229](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/229) by @albertoleon7794 forward, with the mechanism lifted into the framework. The analysis, the attack table and the measured trial behind this are theirs; credited as co-author on the commit. Refs #173.

## The gap

[§4.9.1](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#491-naming-an-exchange-from-outside-the-framework) has required an external citation to name an exchange by the initiating document's `id` since 0.3. An `id` is a **name**. §4.3 obliges a *conforming producer* to mint it unique and never reuse it — and that obligation constrains conforming producers and nobody else. Anyone may write a different document, different parties and different `payload`, and give it the same `id`. A verifier pairing a credential to a document by `id` equality accepts the counterfeit and then reports an event the documents do not attest.

Found from the DTG Core Credentials side, on a Verifiable Witness Credential whose `taskContext` is exactly such a citation.

## What lands

**New §4.9.3.** A citation relied upon outside the exchange **SHOULD** carry a *task digest* over the document it names. Where one is carried the computation is fixed:

```
taskDigest = multibase( multihash( H( JCS( document ∖ proof ) ) ) )
```

Top-level `proof` removed; a `proof` nested inside `payload` is payload content and stays. SHA-256 RECOMMENDED, algorithm declared in-band by the multihash prefix.

**Why `proof` is excluded** — this is the part worth reading. Not a workaround for OPTIONAL proofs: §4.7 *already* defines `proof` as excluded from the content a proof covers. So the digest and the document's own signature commit to the same content, and a document has exactly one task digest whether or not anyone signed it. A digest including `proof` would be undefined for every document §4.7.1 permits to carry none, and would change value at the moment of signing — so a citing party and a verifying party computing it at different points in the document's life would disagree.

**Two implementation traps, stated normatively:**

- Compare **decoded multihash bytes**, never encoded strings. `DigestMultibase` admits both `z` and `u`, so two conforming encodings of one digest are different strings and a string compare rejects a valid pairing. String comparison is the obvious implementation and it is wrong.
- An unimplemented hash algorithm leaves the citation **unverified** — never recomputed under a substitute algorithm, never silently downgraded to `id` comparison.

**What it does not do**, said plainly in a non-normative note rather than left for someone to discover: a task digest attests **content, not authenticity**. It is load-bearing because the *citing artifact* signs it — nobody obtains a signature over a digest of a document the signer never saw — but a `proof`-stripped copy of a genuine document reproduces the same value by design. Authenticity comes from the documents' own proofs under §4.7.1.

## Three digest conventions, now reconciled

The repo had two notions of "the same document" and this adds a third. Left unstated they read as contradictions, so each now points at the others:

| | Question it answers | Top-level `proof` |
|---|---|---|
| §7.2 item 11 / §8.4 — *document identity* | which serialization arrived | **included** (re-signed proof ⇒ different document ⇒ `idConflict`) |
| `trust-ceremony-receipt` — *step digest* | which bytes a party held | **included**, salted |
| §4.9.3 — *task digest* | what the document says | **excluded** |

§4.9.3 states it is not §7.2's identity; `trust-ceremony-receipt`'s bullet — which reasons in the opposite direction, correctly for its own purpose — now says why it differs and points back.

## Applied to the witness specs

Where the gap surfaced, and unchanged in substance from #229:

- **`witness/session`** — names the locator/binder split where it introduces the anchor.
- **`witness/session/submit`** — the VWC's `taskDigestMultibase` MUST be the session document's task digest; the holder ships that document alongside the retained `#response` (the check isn't performable without it); the verifier's pairing checklist gains the digest step with the byte-comparison rule.
- A short non-normative subsection on why `witness/session`'s `proofRequirement.request: OPTIONAL` doesn't weaken the pairing: the digest is a value the **witness** signed into the VWC, and attribution rests on the `#response`'s REQUIRED proof, which is where this spec already put it.
- **Payload schema** — the `vwc` description states the rule, and `vwcDigestMultibase` now says why it covers the credential *including* proof while a task digest excludes it. Same document, two digests, opposite conventions; the next implementer shouldn't have to guess.

## Housekeeping

- No Trust Task wire shape changes. `taskDigestMultibase` is a credential member — schema owned by DTG Core Credentials, amended there. §4.9.3 owns only the computation.
- Additive to framework 0.4; no document member added, no existing citation becomes non-conforming. `targetFrameworkVersion` unaffected.
- Bindings regenerated (Rust + TS); both libraries bumped **0.8.1 → 0.8.2**. Description strings only — no type, constant or wire change. Six dependent crates pin `"0.8"`, so no workspace-wide bump.
- **Drive-by fix:** `trust-tasks-ts/package-lock.json` was stale at `0.6.5` while `package.json` said `0.8.1` — missed in the 0.7.0 bump (#223) and never caught, since no CI check compares them. Now `0.8.2`. Worth a guard separately.

## Sequencing

`taskDigestMultibase` does not exist in a published VWC schema yet — `trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#18` is staged. The witness MUST is unsatisfiable until that lands, so **hold the merge on the credential side**, or land §4.9.3 alone first and gate the witness edits behind it. §4.9.3 stands on its own either way.

## Verification

`npm run validate` (306 specs), `npm run build`, `npm run check-bindings` (306 TS / 301 Rust modules agree), `cargo test --workspace` (490 passed, 0 failed), `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy`, `tsc -p trust-tasks-ts`, `npm test` in `trust-tasks-ts` (43 passed). Pre-existing warnings only.

---

@albertoleon7794 — #229 can close in favour of this if you're happy with where the mechanism ended up; the substance is yours and unchanged, the move is that the computation belongs in §4.9.3 rather than in the witness spec, so the next credential type citing any Trust Task doesn't re-derive it. Note the two traps I added normatively (byte comparison, unsupported-algorithm) — both were reachable from the original text.

title: feat(framework): publish trust-task-ok, the courtesy acknowledgement (§8.6)
body:
Closes the last reserved-but-unspecified slug in §8.6.

## Why it's narrower than §8.6 promised

`trust-task-ok` has been reserved since framework 0.1, with §8.6 offering only *"success with metadata"*. Four revisions of delay turned out to be useful, because the rule that shapes this specification didn't exist when the slug was reserved.

**The gap is real**: 17 specs in the registry are fire-and-forget, define no success-response document, and currently have no way to say "done". A consumer **MAY** now return an acknowledgement for those. It **MUST NOT** be sent in place of a response a specification does define — two success dispositions for one task leave a producer unable to tell which is authoritative.

## The weakness is the design

> A producer **MUST NOT** rely on receiving an acknowledgement, and the absence of one carries **no information**.

This is what makes the specification safe to add at all, and it's the part worth reviewing.

**§7.2 item 11 (from #223) already gives silence a meaning** for fire-and-forget tasks: an absorbed duplicate is not executed again and *"that silence is the correct disposition, not an error."* An acknowledgement a producer could rely on would have made that ambiguous — absorbed duplicate, or lost message? Under the non-reliance rule both readings stay sound: an acknowledgement is informative when it arrives and meaningless when it doesn't.

It also forecloses the failure mode directly: a producer that read absence as failure and reissued a *consequential* task would cause exactly the duplicate effect item 11 exists to prevent.

## What it is not for

An acknowledgement that will be relied on, audited, or disputed is **not** this document. Such a task declares its own success response, or a dedicated receipt task with its own proof requirement.

`chat/message/0.1` already made that call deliberately — deferring to a task-specific receipt so the acknowledgement is *"a signed, independently-verifiable link in the chain rather than a transport-level ack."* The spec cites that choice as correct rather than inviting anyone to reverse it now that a generic option exists.

## Keeping `refs` honest

`payload.refs` carries the "references, receipts, or transient state" of the original §8.6 wording, with one constraint: a consumer **MUST NOT** convey through it anything the originating task's contract depends on. **A producer parsing `refs` to continue an exchange is using the wrong document**, and the task should declare its own `#response`.

Without that line, this member becomes where specifications put things they couldn't be bothered to model.

## `proof` is RECOMMENDED, not REQUIRED

The primary defence against a forged acknowledgement is the non-reliance rule — a producer that may not act on one cannot be induced to act by a false one. The residual harm is to the *record* rather than to behaviour, since these are routinely logged; deployments that retain acknowledgements **SHOULD** require the proof.

## Versioning — a patch, not another workspace event

Libraries go to **0.8.1**. Purely additive in both: a new generated module and its exports, **no hand-written runtime change, no new error code, no widened enum**. The six crates pinned to `0.8` are unaffected, so unlike 0.8.0 this needs no coordinated release.

## Also fixed

The 0.4 changelog entry for `trust-task-next-step` still said `trust-task-ok` "remains reserved" — within the same revision that now publishes it.

## Validation

- `npm run validate` — **306 specs**; `npm run check-bindings` — 306 specs against 306 TS and 301 Rust modules, all agree.
- `cargo build` / `clippy -D warnings` / `fmt --check` / `test --workspace` — clean.
- **43/43** TS tests; `tsc --noEmit` clean; smoke imports the built package (384 exports).
- All 65 SPEC.md anchors resolve.

## AI usage declaration

Drafted with AI assistance, from a design discussion on what the reserved slug should mean.

title: chore(deps): affinidi-messaging-delivery 0.1.14
body:
Takes [affinidi-tdk-rs#710](https://github.com/affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs/pull/710) — the fix for the delivery layer acking a message no consumer received.

## Why this matters here

An ack is a delete at the mediator, and `run_dispatcher` acked unconditionally — including when its subscriber broadcast had just returned `Err`, meaning nobody was listening. Those messages were destroyed.

The window is small and its contents are not: no subscriber is installed for a moment at startup and again on the way down, and what arrives then is whatever the peer happened to send. **For the VTC that's a join submit or a credential-exchange reply; for the VTA, a trust task.** It surfaced first in OpenVTC (its #221) only because that's where a lost membership credential is visible to a human — the same window exists on both services here.

## What changed

**Lockfile only.** The requirement was already `"0.1.12"`, so 0.1.14 satisfies it and no manifest moves. But resolution is the point: the fix landing upstream does nothing for a build still resolving 0.1.13 from crates.io, which is what this workspace was doing.

## Verified

- `cargo build --workspace` clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` — the exact CI invocation — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` clean
- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vti-e2e-tests` passes

## Pre-existing failure worth knowing about (not from this PR)

If you run clippy with `--all-targets` locally it fails:

```
error: use of deprecated method `vta_sdk::client::backup::…::backup_export`:
       inline export rides a legacy protocol message with no TSP path
       — use the descriptor flow (backup/initiate-export)
  --> tests/e2e/tests/client_didcomm.rs:1154:22
```

I confirmed this is **already on main** with an unmodified tree — `vta-sdk 0.24` deprecated `backup_export`, and that arrived with the release, not with this bump. CI runs `cargo clippy --workspace` without `--all-targets`, so it isn't caught there. Migrating that test to the descriptor flow is worth its own change; I've deliberately not folded it in here.

title: docs(specs): state authorization evidence for the remaining consequential specs
body:
Completes the §7.3 item 15 sweep begun in #220 and #221.

## Scope

25 specs that named an authority-bearing role in front-matter `parties[]` — `Administrator`, `Key custodian`, `ACL maintainer`, `Issuing authority`, `community maintainer` — without the prose saying what a consumer must establish.

**None is non-conforming.** Item 15 binds specifications targeting framework 0.4; these target 0.1 and 0.2, so each declaration is marked as *anticipating* the requirement, the same treatment #221 gave.

After this, **180 of 182** consequential specs carry the section. The two that don't are `did-management/domain/disable/0.1` and `push/register/0.1`, both `retired` and therefore frozen by §5.3.

## A correction to my own audit heading

The finding that produced this list was partly wrong about *why*. The `parties[]` role that made these look under-specified is usually the **recipient** — the ACL maintainer, the custodian, the community maintainer *receiving* the request — not the party whose authority is at issue.

Most of these specs did describe their authority. They described it in per-spec domain vocabulary, scattered through Conformance, with no conventional place to look. `acl/revoke` already said *"either the subject themselves (self-revoke) or a party authorized to remove the subject"*; `keys/derive-and-sign` already said *"decide, from its own policy, whether this producer may derive and sign at this path"*. **This sweep is mostly about location and consistency, not filling voids.**

## Three where the check really was absent

**`vta/credentials/revoke/0.1`** — the clearest gap in the set. `destructive`, and its consumer conformance only validated the proof and reported `not_found` / `already_revoked`. Both are statements about *credential state*, so a consumer returning them without first establishing standing tells an unauthorized caller whether a credential exists and whether it is live. Now names the evidence, and adds that the refusal **SHOULD NOT** distinguish an unknown credential from one the caller may not revoke.

**`acl/change-role/0.1`** — verified the proof and the `fromRole` precondition, neither of which is an authorization question; `state_mismatch` is a concurrency failure.

**`did-management/domain/*` and `registry/*`** — "Admin caller emits" names who the task expects, not anything the document proves, and no consumer-side check was stated.

## What else the sections record

Several existing refusals are easy to mistake for authorization checks and are not. Worth stating once rather than leaving each implementer to work out:

- `acl/revoke:last_authority_protected` fires **after** the caller is authorized, and protects the resulting ACL state.
- `vtc/admin/bootstrap`'s `alreadyBootstrapped` is what bounds a single-use setup token to exactly one administrator — there is no administrator to authorize that call, since creating the first one is what it does.
- `vtc/relationships/revoke` returns `notFound` to a non-issuer **deliberately**, as an anti-probing measure; distinguishing it from a genuine miss would let a caller enumerate relationships it did not issue.
- `vtc/members/rotate` requires **both** signatures because either alone permits a hostile transfer — one steals a membership, the other strands it on a key nobody holds.

## Validation

- `npm run validate` / `npm run build` — pass, 305 specs unchanged.
- All relative `SPEC.md` links verified to resolve across all 25 files (depths range from 4 to 6 levels).
- Re-ran the audit: IMPLICIT 24 → 1, SILENT 3 → 1, both remaining being the frozen retired specs.
- Prose only, in place, no new versions per §5.2's draft errata rule. No schema or generated code touched — no library regeneration or version bump.

## AI usage declaration

Drafted with AI assistance, from a read of each spec's existing conformance rules and error codes; the authority described for each is the one already implemented there.

title: vta-service-v0.16.0
body:
### Added

- **vta-vault**: Bind an mdoc to the VTA key that can present it ([#990](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/990))

An mdoc's holder binding is a key, not a DID: the MSO carries a deviceKey, and
  only its private half can sign DeviceAuth. Nothing in the stored envelope said
  which VTA key that was, so a received mdoc could be stored and then turn out to
  be unpresentable — with the failure surfacing much later, at presentation, and
  nothing pointing at the cause.

  Receive now resolves that binding and refuses the credential if this VTA does
  not hold the key. Storing a credential you can never present is a trap, and the
  right moment to find out is the moment it arrives.

  mdoc_device_key_sec1 extracts the MSO deviceKey as a compressed SEC1 point —
  the same encoding the VTA stores its own P-256 public keys in — so the caller
  can compare without re-deriving either side. Extraction lives in vta-vault
  because it reads mdoc internals; the matching lives in vta-service because that
  is the layer that can see the keyspace. vta-vault does not depend on vta-keys,
  and this keeps it that way.

  find_key_by_public_multibase is a linear scan: the keyspace is indexed by key
  id, not by public key, and a reverse index for one receive-path caller is not
  worth the write amplification on every mint. It takes no AuthClaims because it
  answers a factual question, not an authorization one — the caller gates on the
  returned record's context_id, because binding a credential to a key in a
  context the caller cannot act in would be a cross-tenant escape.

- **vta-service**: Accept ISO mdoc over the credential-receive Trust Task ([#989](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/989))

Everything shipped for mdoc so far — the format identity ([#984](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/984)), receive-side
  verification ([#986](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/986)) and the IACA trust anchors ([#987](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/987)) — was reachable only
  through the library. handle_receive was hardcoded to the Data-Integrity path:
  a JSON credential, an issuer DID resolved through the DID cache, no format
  parameter. An mdoc could not arrive at the VTA at all. This connects it.

  ReceiveBody gains an optional format tag and a credentialBase64 carrier, since
  an mdoc is CBOR and cannot travel as JSON. Absent format still means
  Data-Integrity, which is the shape every existing client sends, so a deployed
  wallet is unaffected — pinned by a test that parses a pre-existing body and
  asserts it still routes to the DI path. Exactly one of credential or
  credentialBase64 must be present; both, or neither, is a malformedRequest.

  The mdoc arm is where the two credential families genuinely diverge. A DI
  credential names its issuer as a DID and the key is resolved through the cache;
  an mdoc names its issuer as an X.509 Document Signer, so the credential is
  decoded first to read its x5chain and the key comes from the configured IACA
  anchors instead. That asymmetry is the whole reason the anchors exist.

  AppState carries the parsed anchors, built once in build_app_state from
  [vault] mdoc_iaca_trust_anchors. A malformed certificate fails the boot rather
  than surfacing as a puzzling rejection on the first mdoc that arrives. Empty is
  legal and means this VTA accepts no mdoc issuers; the resolver fails closed on
  it, so wiring the wire surface does not by itself make any VTA start trusting
  mdocs — an operator still has to configure anchors deliberately.

  No schema change: vault/credentials/receive/0.1 is in UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS,
  so there is no published payload schema to update and dispatch validation is a
  no-op for it either way.

  Note for a follow-up, not changed here: test_support.rs constructs an AppState
  literal directly, so build_app_state is not in practice the single constructor
  its doc comment claims. Adding a field has to be done in both places.

  id, not by public key, and a reverse index for one receive-path caller is not
  worth the write amplification on every mint. It takes no AuthClaims because it
  answers a factual question, not an authorization one — the caller gates on the
  returned record's context_id, because binding a credential to a key in a
  context the caller cannot act in would be a cross-tenant escape.

- **vta-vault**: Resolve mdoc issuers against configured IACA trust anchors ([#987](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/987))

Answers the one question mdoc asks differently from every other credential
  format here: which key do I trust to have issued this?

  Every other format names its issuer as a DID, so receiving resolves that DID
  and verifies against whatever comes back — the VTA holds no list and there is
  no operator step. An mdoc has no issuer DID. It carries an X.509 chain in the
  issuerAuth COSE unprotected header (x5chain, label 33): a Document Signer
  certificate issued by an IACA. Verifying it means the VTA must already hold the
  roots it accepts, which is a trust store, not a lookup.

  The decision taken is a configured set of IACA root certificates — how
  production EUDI verifiers work, and what Member State trusted lists (ETSI TS
  119 612) distribute. It keeps X.509 at the boundary: nothing below this module
  learns certificates exist, and receive_mdoc still takes a plain resolved key.

  Validation is scoped to what ISO 18013-5 Annex B actually specifies — a
  two-level IACA to Document Signer hierarchy, so no general RFC 5280 path
  building. Checks the leaf issuer DN against a configured anchor subject, the
  leaf signature against that anchor key, the leaf validity window, that the
  anchor is a CA (a DS certificate configured by mistake cannot become a root),
  and keyUsage.digitalSignature where present.

  Deliberately not checked, both documented in the module: revocation (CRL/OCSP
  needs egress and an unavailability policy — its own decision), and the ISO mDL
  EKU 1.0.18013.5.1.2, which the EUDI PID profile does not share, so enforcing it
  would reject valid PID credentials as what looks exactly like a trust failure.

  Fails closed. An empty anchor set is an error, not permissive — mdoc is the one
  format whose issuer is not a resolvable DID, so there is no safe default. The
  config field defaults to empty, so an existing config still loads and an upgrade
  neither breaks a deployment nor silently starts trusting mdocs.

  Anchors are inline PEM in [vault] rather than file paths: an enclave has no
  convenient filesystem, and inline values are covered by the effective-config
  digest boot attestation commits to, so a verifier can see which issuers a TEE
  VTA was trusting when it was attested.

  x509-parser takes the verify-aws feature rather than the default verify, which
  pulls ring — ring currently only reaches this workspace through a
  dev-dependency, while aws-lc-rs is already a real dependency. Same crypto, no
  new production tree.

title: docs: warn about the third hand-maintained sync list
body:
Found while adding `trust-task-control` in #232.

`specs/spec.meta.schema.json` carries an allowlist at `#/properties/slug/anyOf[1]/enum` naming the framework slugs permitted to use the namespace SPEC §6.1 reserves. Publishing a new one means updating **both** that enum and the §6.1 table — and CLAUDE.md warned about the two analogous lists (categories in `data.js`, bindings in `bindings.js`) but not this one.

**The build does catch a missing entry**, so unlike the `data.js` trap nothing ships broken. But it fails with:

```
- trust-task-control/0.1/spec.md: /slug must NOT be valid
- trust-task-control/0.1/spec.md: /slug must be equal to one of the allowed values
```

which is the schema saying *"your slug hit the reservation and is not on the allowlist"* in the least helpful way available — and it names the spec file rather than the list that actually needs editing. The new section says which two files to touch and what the failure looks like, so the next person recognises it immediately.

Relevant soon: `trust-task-ok` is still reserved-but-unpublished (§8.6), so whoever specifies it will hit this exact wall.

Docs only.

title: feat(framework): specify task control — cancel, suspend, resume (§12)
body:
Closes #204. Implements the design agreed on the issue and recorded in [`task-control-and-corrigibility.md`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/docs/design-notes/task-control-and-corrigibility.md) (#227, revised in #231).

## The gap

The framework could express what should happen *next* — `parentThreadId`, ceremonies, `trust-task-next-step` — but nothing let a producer take a request **back**. For long-running and agentic execution that's a corrigibility gap: an agent could be told to start and had no defined way to be told to stop. Transport-level cancellation isn't a substitute, since a document that's been accepted, queued, or forwarded outlives the connection that delivered it.

## Why this is small

Three rules added earlier in this revision already do most of the work. §12.3 states explicitly what the design note identified as load-bearing, and what @sankarshanmukhopadhyay asked be made explicit rather than inferred:

> **A received, authorized control operation is one of the conditions §7.2 item 12 re-evaluates before each irreversible effect.**

Item 12 then already requires the subsequent effect not be performed, and partial execution be reported distinguishably. **No separate race protocol was needed.** Item 11's per-`id` record serves as the tombstone for a control document arriving before the task it names, on the same acceptance-window bound. Item 10 settles who may ask.

## Decisions

| | |
|---|---|
| **Authorization** | A **floor, not a ceiling** — target's `issuer` by default, any other party under item 10. An absolute rule would foreclose mandate holders and supervising principals at framework level, where every other authorization decision belongs to the consumer |
| **Rollback** | Never. Many effects are irreversible by construction, and the state needed to reverse one is often the material the task existed to destroy — keeping a superseded private key so a rotation could be undone defeats the rotation. The response reports what occurred instead |
| **Suspension** | Preserves execution state rather than rewinding. `MUST NOT` resume after `expiresAt` — resumption is item 4's acceptance question asked again, while execution under way stays protected by item 12's exclusion of expiry |
| **Silence** | Carries no information. Notifications are fire-and-forget and support is optional, so reading silence as "safely abandoned" and reissuing causes the second effect item 11 exists to prevent |
| **`supersede`** | Deferred — largely cancel-plus-a-new-document |

`cancelled` (§8.3) is new, for a consumer stopping on its own initiative, carried by `trust-task-error/0.5`. Distinct from a producer-requested cancellation, which is answered by a response to the control document — without that, no party and no auditor could tell a withdrawal from a refusal, and the two imply opposite things about whether to retry.

## Two findings worth carrying forward

**`specs/spec.meta.schema.json` holds a third hand-maintained list that must track SPEC §6.1** — the allowlist of framework slugs permitted in the reserved namespace. It isn't among the sync traps CLAUDE.md warns about (categories, bindings), and the build fails on a missing entry with `/slug must NOT be valid` rather than explaining what's wrong. Worth adding to CLAUDE.md separately.

**The Rust generator (typify) doesn't support `if/then/else` schemas.** My first draft expressed "`effects` is required where `outcome` is `appliedWithEffects`" as a conditional and the codegen panicked. It's now carried in prose and in Conformance instead — noted in the schema description so the next author doesn't retry it.

## Versioning

Libraries move to **0.8.0 together**. Adding a standard code is *additive in Rust* — `StandardCode` has been `#[non_exhaustive]` since 0.7.0, and **`trust-tasks-https` compiled unchanged**, which is that decision paying for itself one release later — but it widens the TypeScript string-literal union and so breaks exhaustive switches there. Kept in step per CLAUDE.md rather than diverging.

`cancelled` maps to **HTTP 422** in `trust-tasks-https` and its binding table: a deliberate stop is neither a server fault nor a malformed request, which is the same reasoning as `taskFailed`.

## Validation

- `npm run validate` — **305 specs** (was 303: `trust-task-control/0.1` and `trust-task-error/0.5`).
- `npm run check-bindings` — 305 specs against 305 TS and 300 Rust modules, all agree.
- `cargo build` / `clippy -D warnings` / `fmt --check` / `test --workspace` — clean, 33 test groups.
- **43/43** TS runtime tests; `tsc --noEmit` clean; smoke imports the built package (383 exports).
- Both generators reproduce committed output; the only non-generated deltas are the hand-written `_runtime/*.ts`, `error.rs`, `document.rs`, `status.rs`.
- All 63 SPEC.md anchors resolve after the §12 insertion and the §13/§14 renumbering.

## AI usage declaration

Drafted with AI assistance, from a design agreed on #204. Declared for symmetry with the originating issue.
