title: feat(ceremony): support the offline bilateral shape, and stop over-fitting to VTC
body:
Committee feedback against an offline two-person protocol found three rules that only hold when a maintainer is present. Each is fine for the shape the note was tested against — **that is the finding**.

Every flow in the corpus is **mediated**: VTC onboarding, `task-consent`, `credential-exchange` all have a maintainer or community always present and always online. Three properties of that *sample* were written down as properties of *ceremonies*.

The uncomfortable part: ADR 0001 chose "ceremony" for its security-literature sense — a protocol extended to include **human participants**, as in a key-signing ceremony. Two people meeting in person is the most ceremony-shaped interaction there is, and it was the one shape the design could not express.

## Demonstrated, not asserted

Running a mutual-attestation definition through the publication checker:

```
mutual prev          -> "prev graph has a cycle" + "nothing can open the enactment"
two prev-less steps  -> "2 required steps have empty prev; deadline origin ambiguous"
```

Inexpressible, not merely awkward.

## The three fixes

**`coDerived` anchor (§7.3).** `prev` does two jobs — causal dependency, and the origin the enactment is measured from. A simultaneous exchange has the second without the first. A definition now declares its anchor: `openingStep` (default, every mediated flow) or `coDerived`, where the anchor is the enactment identifier itself, jointly derived by the roles in `boundBy` from something neither party could produce alone. Since `ceremony.enactment` is signed, every step signing it *is* every step committing to the shared anchor. An anchor bound by one role is rejected — that is an opening step wearing a disguise.

**Bilateral `countersigned` (§7.5–7.6).** "Far too heavy as a default" is true of a twelve-step mediated flow and backwards for two people, who are present and signing anyway. It was also listed as needing a definition because "the participant set must be known"; in a bilateral ceremony it is evident from the documents — so such an enactment verifies with **no definition**, which is what makes it work with no network *at verification time*, not merely at enactment time.

**Issuance-window `maxDuration` (§9).** The draft rejected a step "arriving after the deadline", conflating a **stale command** with a **settled record**. A ceremony that completed inside its window stays complete however long its documents took to travel — and offline, they travel late by design. `now` never enters the comparison.

The companion rule requiring a steps `expiresAt` to fall inside the deadline is **dropped, not repaired**: it defended against replay into a closed enactment, which signing `ceremony.enactment` already prevents outright. A rule duplicating a stronger guarantee only creates ways to be wrong.

## Layering (§2.3), from the second feedback batch

> A ceremony **MUST NOT** mandate what is verified or created by its steps.

A definition names Type URIs; what those tasks carry — DTG credentials, acknowledgements, nothing — belongs to those specifications. Two ceremonies producing entirely different artifacts, or none, are the same kind of object. The corollary matters more than the rule: **a ceremonys evidence and an artifacts validity are separate questions.** A design that let a ceremony vouch for credentials minted inside it would have made every ceremony a certificate authority.

## Referencing a ceremony from outside it (§10.1)

§4.9.1 (name an exchange by its initiating document `id`) and §4.11.2 (name a flow by its `enactment`) are **different scopes**. A context field bound to `threadId` can express *"came out of that task"* and cannot express *"came out of that ceremony"*.

Three consequences an external specification must decide for itself: completion evidence is not artifact validity; **participation is not authority** (§4.11.4 and §7.2 item 9 already say so for the envelope member); and an enactment identifier embedded in a durable artifact is a worse correlation handle than in a step, because a credential may be shown for years to anyone — cite a commitment the holder can open selectively.

## Enforcement and evidence

- `anchor` in the definition format; `maxDuration` redocumented as an issuance window
- Checker: opener rule respects anchor kind, `countersigned` + recorders rejected, bilateral countersigned reported as verifiable from step documents alone
- **`ceremonies/mutual-attestation/0.1`** — a real definition of the offline shape, validating, built only from Type URIs the registry serves
- Fixtures **14 → 18**, with per-case `base` so anchor rules test the shape they govern, and each base asserted to pass before its mutations are trusted

One fixture failed on first run and was right to: my "every step follows another under a coDerived anchor" check was **unreachable** — such a graph is either a cycle or names a missing step, both already caught — and the fixture asserted a legitimate ordered pair was invalid. Check and fixture both removed.

§16 gains a fourth round, and it is the only one that needed someone outside the corpus.

title: fix(ts-bindings): identify a schema's root type by title, not by position
body:
> Stacked on #214 — base retargets to `main` automatically when that merges. The diff here is this change alone.

Found while regenerating for #214. **`Payload` aliases the wrong type in the TypeScript bindings for 14 published specifications.**

`rootTypeName()` took the first `export interface|type` in the compiled output, on the assumption that the root always comes first. It does not: where a schema `$ref`s a shared definition, json-schema-to-typescript may hoist that definition to its own exported type *ahead of* the root, and the first-match rule picked it up. So `chat/message/0.1`, `trust-ceremony-receipt/0.1`, `consent/request/1.0`, both `audit/*`, all three `task-consent/*` — and `vrc/relationships/issue/0.1` and `witness/session/submit/0.1`, published yesterday in #213 — each exported:

```ts
export type Payload = DigestMultibase;   // = string
```

in place of their request payload interface.

## Why nothing caught it

Worth stating, because the same gap will hide the next one:

- **The drift check compares the generator's output to itself.** A consistently wrong alias is consistently wrong, so drift is clean.
- **`tsc --noEmit` is satisfied** — the alias is well-formed TypeScript.
- **No test asserts what `Payload` resolves to.**

Same failure mode as the response-type drop fixed in #174, and it survived for the same reason: the rule that had to be right was a positional guess about compiler output.

## The fix

The root is identified by the name the compiler derives from the schema's own `title` — the same derivation json-schema-to-typescript uses — and only where that name is actually present in the emitted output. Position remains the fallback for a schema carrying no usable title.

A positional guess replaced by a better guess is still a guess, so this carries **an invariant**: an object-rooted schema whose root resolves to a *bare* alias (`= string`, `= DigestMultibase`) now fails the build, because that is the shape this failure always takes.

Scoped to bare aliases deliberately. An earlier draft rejected any `export type` root and took out `auth/revoke-session`, `credential-exchange/issue` and `keys/import`, which legitimately compile to `export type X = { … }` — an object type literal, and a union, are both valid root forms. The narrowed check leaves those alone.

## Versioning

**Not treated as a breaking change**, despite changing compile-visible types on 14 specs. The old alias was unusable: assigning a real payload to a `string` does not compile, so no correct consumer could have depended on it — the only code that compiled against it was code passing a string, which meant nothing. Bumped **0.6.3 → 0.6.4**.

The Rust bindings were never affected (`pub struct Payload` is generated from a different path). `trust-tasks-rs` 0.6.4 is unchanged in content and moves only to keep the two libraries in step, per CLAUDE.md's convention — no dependent-crate version requirements move.

## Verification

`npm run build-ts-bindings` emits **349 modules, none dropped**; **zero** bare-alias `Payload` exports remain, down from 14. `npm run validate` green at 298 specs, `tsc --noEmit` clean, TS suite 43/43, `cargo test --workspace`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo fmt` green, and `git diff trust-tasks-rs/src` is empty.

Refs #173. Stacked on #214.

title: feat(specs): converge the remaining bare-hex digests onto DigestMultibase
body:
Finishes the sweep #214 began. Two bare lowercase-hex SHA-256 members were left in the registry, both scoped out there because their blast radius was larger and their defect narrower:

| Spec | Member | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `vault/_shared` | `VaultEntry.attachments[].sha256` | `digestMultibase` |
| `provision/integration` | `summary.digest` | `digestMultibase` |

**No bare-hex digest now remains in any current specification version.**

## The defect, and what it is *not*

Both hard-coded one algorithm into the wire contract — moving off SHA-256 would need a schema revision rather than a different multihash prefix — and named no base encoding, leaving a verifier to infer base16 from context.

Unlike the credential digests in #214, both are taken over **opaque bytes** rather than a JSON document, so **no canonicalization defect is being fixed here**. #214's third and worst problem — three specs promising the same value with no way to guarantee it — does not apply. This is the encoding argument alone, and each new description now states what its digest is computed over so the distinction stays on the record rather than being re-litigated.

Where it does bite: under `provision/integration`'s **`pinnedOnly`** assertion mode this digest is the holder's *sole* integrity anchor for the sealed bundle. An anchor whose algorithm is fixed by the schema cannot be strengthened without breaking every holder that already pinned one.

## Why this PR has the shape it does

The vault change arrives through a **shared component**, and [§5.4](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#54-migrating-between-versions)'s coupling rule says a specification cannot adopt a new shared component version without issuing a new version of itself. So `vault/_shared/0.3` carries the converged `AttachmentRef`, and the three specs that expose `VaultEntry` — and therefore its attachment digests — bump with it: **`vault/get/0.3`, `vault/list/0.3`, `vault/upsert/0.3`**.

**`vault/proxy-login` and `vault/release` deliberately stay on `_shared/0.2`.** They reference only `SiteTarget` and `SecretKind`, never reach an attachment digest, and §5.4 explicitly permits a specification to remain pinned to the older component rather than bump for a change it does not carry. Bumping them would have been churn dressed as thoroughness.

## Deliberately not converged

**`AndroidApp.sha256CertFingerprints`**, in the very same shared file. Its colon-separated uppercase hex is Google's format — emitted by `apksigner` and the Play Console, and matched against an app's actual signing certificate. That is an **externally-owned value**, carried verbatim per [SPEC §4.10](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#410-naming-conventions). Converting it would break the only thing it exists to compare against. Flagging it explicitly so a later sweep doesn't "finish the job".

## Versioning

Breaking on the wire, released as `MINOR` increments under [§5.2](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#52-compatibility-rules)'s `draft` allowance. Every superseded version stays published, pinned and generated, so this is **additive to the libraries** — `0.6.4 → 0.6.5`.

`provision/integration/0.3` also drops `0.2`'s `wireCompatibleWith: "0.1"`, which no longer holds: `0.3` is wire-identical to neither. All four specs move to `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.4"`.

Each new version carries a **Changes from 0.2** section with the reasoning and the §5.4 migration sequence.

## Verification

`npm run validate` green at **302 specs / 60 shared schemas**; both drift checks clean; `cargo test --workspace`, `cargo test --features validate`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo fmt`, `tsc --noEmit` and the TS suite (43/43) green. Confirmed the superseded versions are byte-identical (`git diff` on `_shared/0.2`, `get/0.2`, `integration/0.2` is empty), and that #215's root-type fix holds on the new modules — `Payload` aliases to the real interface on all four.

Refs #173. Follows #214.

title: feat(framework): separate authorization from identity and proof validation (§7.2 item 10)
body:
Closes #205.

## What

Generalizes the identity/proof-versus-authorization boundary from the two narrow places the framework already states it to every Trust Task, and names the class of task the stricter rules apply to.

- **§2** — defines *consequential Trust Task* as `sideEffects.level ∈ {mutating, destructive} ∨ exposure.discloses = secret ∨ exposure.actsAsSubject = true`, with the fail-safe reading of an absent or unresolvable declaration folded in.
- **§7.2 item 10** — a consumer **MUST NOT** treat successful validation of a VID, `issuer`, `recipient`, transport-derived identity, or `proof` as establishing that anyone is authorized to request or perform the task, and **MUST** evaluate authorization separately before executing.
- **§7.3 item 15** — a consequential specification **MUST** describe the class of authorization evidence it presupposes, under the same descriptive-not-prescriptive discipline as items 13 and 14.
- **§4.11.4 and §7.2 item 9** — retargeted at item 10 so the ceremony rule reads as an instance of the general rule rather than a competing statement.
- **Appendix B** — 0.4 changelog entries.

## Why

The principle is already in the spec twice: ceremony membership grants nothing (§4.11.4, §7.2 item 9), and the side-effect and exposure classes describe a task without authorizing it (§7.3 items 13–14). It was never stated for an ordinary Trust Task, which leaves an implementer free to read

> valid `proof` + recognized `issuer` + correct `recipient` = authorized instruction

That is the confused-deputy vector §4.11.4 forecloses, reached by a different route. It matters most where the producer is an autonomous agent: such a producer can prove its own identity perfectly while holding no authority to act for a subject, exercise a delegated capability, disclose information, or cause a consequential effect.

## Design decisions worth reviewing

**The rule is model-neutral.** It requires that an authorization decision be *made*, not how. The framework prescribes no delegation, consent, capability or governance model, and item 10 does not constrain which evidence a consumer consults.

**The `task-consent` carve-out is preserved explicitly.** A verified assertion may still *be* the authorization — that is the whole point of `task-consent/decision/0.1`, where the proof on the decision, not the session that carried it, is the authorization. Item 10 permits this only where the specification defines that role *and* the consumer's policy accepts it, so it is a deliberate design a spec adopts, not a default a consumer may infer. §7.3 item 15 gives it a declaration site.

**§7.2 item 10 is appended, not inserted.** SPEC.md, the bindings and the specs collectively reference §7.2 items 5, 7 and 9 by number; appending leaves every existing reference correct.

**§7.3 item 15 is a prose declaration with no front-matter field.** The issue's suggested text could be read as adding a machine-checked declaration. I deliberately did not: that would mean a `spec.meta.schema.json` change, a build-validation change, and re-auditing ~30 spec families before CI goes green. Item 15 says so explicitly so nobody adds the field by accident. If we do want it machine-checked, that should be its own PR.

## Scope / follow-ups

- **§7.3 item 15 is a new MUST on consequential specifications**, and existing specs have not been audited against it. Most already describe their expected authority in prose, but that has not been verified spec-by-spec. Worth a follow-up issue rather than blocking this one.
- The remaining four issues in this batch (#202, #203, #204, #206) all depend on the `consequential` definition landed here; #204 in particular depends on item 10 for the "who may cancel" question.
- SPEC.md's header still reads **Document version 0.3** while Appendix B has an open 0.4 section. Pre-existing, not touched here.

## Validation

- `npm run validate` — passes; 302 specs validated, 410 example documents checked. The three `vta/did-templates` warnings and the one unparsed fenced block are pre-existing and unrelated.
- All internal anchors added by this change resolve.
- §7.3's ordered list confirmed contiguous 1–15 through the indented continuation paragraphs.

title: Generalize the identity/proof-versus-authorization boundary across all Trust Tasks
body:
## Summary

The current framework already contains an important authorization boundary for Trust Ceremonies.

§4.11.4 states that ceremony membership is a claim rather than a permission, and §7.2 item 9 says a consumer **MUST NOT** grant authority on the basis of ceremony membership alone. It further states that authorization decisions rest on `issuer`, `proof`, and the consumer's own policy.

§7.3 also makes clear that side-effect and exposure declarations are descriptive and do not themselves authorize execution.

These are useful safeguards.

The remaining ambiguity is that the framework does not state the identity/proof-versus-authorization boundary equally explicitly for an ordinary Trust Task request outside ceremony membership.

Successful verification of an `issuer`, VID, transport-derived identity, or document `proof` establishes important facts about identity and document integrity. Those facts do not necessarily establish that the producer is authorized to request the described outcome or that the consumer is authorized to execute it.

At the same time, the repository's `task-consent` work demonstrates an important nuance: a verified proof **can** constitute authorization evidence where an individual Trust Task specification and the consumer's policy explicitly give the signed assertion that meaning.

The framework would benefit from making this distinction general.

## Impact of the issue identified

Without a general statement, an implementer could infer:

> valid proof + recognized issuer + correct recipient = authorized instruction.

That inference is particularly risky for agentic and delegated execution.

An agent may be able to prove its own identity while lacking authority to:

- act for a subject;
- exercise a delegated capability;
- disclose information;
- mutate protected state; or
- cause a destructive action.

The current ceremony-specific language substantially reduces this risk inside ceremonies, but the same principle should apply consistently to all Trust Tasks.

## Suggested path to resolution

Generalize the authorization-separation principle already present in §4.11.4 and §7.2 item 9.

The framework should remain authorization-policy neutral. It need not prescribe a particular delegation, consent, capability, or governance model.

The required invariant is narrower:

> identity and proof validation are evidence inputs; they do not automatically establish execution authority unless the applicable task specification and consumer policy explicitly define the verified assertion as authorization evidence.

Individual consequential Trust Task specifications should describe the class of authority expected where that is necessary for interoperability, while leaving the final authorization decision to the consumer and applicable governance framework.

## Suggested normative text

Add to §7.2 Consumer requirements:

> **Authorization is distinct from identity and document-proof validation.** Successful validation of a VID, `issuer`, `recipient`, transport-derived identity, or document `proof` **MUST NOT**, by itself, be interpreted as establishing that the *producer* is authorized to request the outcome described by the *Trust Task* or that the *consumer* is authorized to perform it.
>
> A verified assertion **MAY** constitute authorization evidence where the applicable *Trust Task specification* explicitly defines that semantic role and the *consumer*'s policy accepts the assertion for that purpose.
>
> Before executing a *Trust Task*, a *consumer* **MUST** evaluate any authorization requirements applicable under the individual *Trust Task specification*, the consumer's own policy, and the applicable trust or governance framework.
>
> Such evaluation **MAY** include delegation, mandate, capability, membership, standing, credential status, subject relationship, purpose limitation, or other authorization evidence.
>
> Failure of authorization after successful document validation **SHOULD** be reported as `permissionDenied` where an error response can be returned safely.

Add to §7.3 Specification requirements:

> A specification whose successful execution can cause a consequential side effect, disclose a secret, or act on behalf of a subject **MUST** describe any class of authorization evidence that is necessary to interpret the task correctly. Such a declaration **MUST NOT** be interpreted as requiring a consumer to authorize execution merely because the described evidence is present.

## AI usage declaration

The text content of this issue was developed with the assistance of AI tools for editing and formatting. This is being declared for transparency even though the Working Group / Task Force has not published guidance requiring or prescribing disclosure of AI-tool usage in issue submissions.

title: feat(framework): separate authorization from identity and proof validation (§7.2 item 10) (#218)
body:
feat(framework): separate authorization from identity and proof validation (§7.2 item 10) (#218)

* feat(specs): converge the remaining bare-hex digests onto DigestMultibase

Finishes the sweep #214 began. Two bare lowercase-hex SHA-256 members were left
in the registry, both flagged as out of scope there because their blast radius
was larger and their defect narrower:

  vault/_shared        VaultEntry.attachments[].sha256   -> digestMultibase
  provision/integration  summary.digest                  -> digestMultibase

Both hard-coded one algorithm into the wire contract — moving off SHA-256 would
need a schema revision rather than a different multihash prefix — and named no
base encoding, leaving a verifier to infer base16 from context. Unlike the
credential digests in #214, both are taken over opaque BYTES rather than a JSON
document, so no canonicalization defect is being fixed here; this is the
encoding argument alone, and each new description says what its digest is
computed over so the distinction is on the record.

It matters most under provision's `pinnedOnly` assertion mode, where the digest
is the holder's SOLE integrity anchor for the sealed bundle. An anchor whose
algorithm is fixed by the schema cannot be strengthened without breaking every
holder that already pinned one.

The vault change arrives through a shared component, which decides the shape of
this PR. `vault/_shared/0.3` carries the converged AttachmentRef, and per SPEC
§5.4's coupling rule a specification cannot adopt a new shared component version
without issuing a new version of itself — so the three specs that expose
`VaultEntry`, and therefore its attachment digests, bump with it:

  vault/get/0.3, vault/list/0.3, vault/upsert/0.3

`vault/proxy-login` and `vault/release` deliberately stay on `_shared/0.2`. They
reference only `SiteTarget` and `SecretKind`, never reach an attachment digest,
and §5.4 explicitly permits a specification to remain pinned to the older
component rather than bump for a change it does not carry. Bumping them would
have been churn dressed as thoroughness.

Deliberately NOT converged: `AndroidApp.sha256CertFingerprints` in the same
shared file. Its colon-separated uppercase hex is Google's format, emitted by
apksigner and the Play Console and matched against an app's actual signature —
an externally-owned value, carried verbatim per SPEC §4.10. Converting it would
break the only thing it exists to compare against.

`provision/integration/0.3` also drops `0.2`'s `wireCompatibleWith: "0.1"`,
which no longer holds: `0.3` is wire-identical to neither.

Breaking on the wire, released as MINOR increments under SPEC §5.2's `draft`
allowance; every superseded version remains published, pinned and generated, so
this is additive to the libraries. All four specs move to
targetFrameworkVersion 0.4. Bindings regenerated (302 specs, 60 shared schemas,
both drift checks clean); libraries bumped 0.6.4 -> 0.6.5.

No bare-hex digest now remains in any current specification version.

Refs #173. Follows #214.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(framework): separate authorization from identity and proof validation

The framework stated the identity-is-not-authorization principle twice in
narrow forms — ceremony membership grants nothing (§4.11.4, §7.2 item 9),
and the side-effect and exposure classes describe a task without
authorizing it (§7.3 items 13 and 14) — but never for an ordinary Trust
Task. That left an implementer free to read "valid proof + recognized
issuer + correct recipient" as an authorized instruction, which is the
confused-deputy vector §4.11.4 forecloses, reached by a different route.
It matters most where the producer is an autonomous agent: such a producer
can prove its own identity perfectly while holding no authority to act for
a subject, exercise a delegated capability, or cause a consequential effect.

§7.2 gains item 10, appended rather than inserted so the existing
references to items 5, 7 and 9 keep their numbering. The rule is
model-neutral: it requires that an authorization decision be made, not how.
A verified assertion may still *be* the authorization where a specification
defines that role and the consumer's policy accepts it — the task-consent
design — but that is now an explicit declaration rather than a default a
consumer may infer.

§7.3 gains item 15, requiring a consequential specification to describe the
class of authorization evidence it presupposes, under the same
descriptive-not-prescriptive discipline as items 13 and 14. It is satisfied
in prose and has no front-matter field, so spec.meta.schema.json and the
build are untouched.

§2 gains *consequential Trust Task*, naming the predicate
sideEffects.level in {mutating, destructive} or exposure.discloses = secret
or exposure.actsAsSubject = true once instead of re-spelling it at each use,
with the fail-safe reading of an absent declaration folded in.

Additive: the wire format is unchanged, every document conforming to 0.3
still conforms, and no payload or framework schema changes, so the
generated libraries need no regeneration or version bump.

Refs #205

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: feat(bindings): didcomm-v1/0.2 — move the carriage to a dedicated message type
body:
`bindings/didcomm-v1/0.1` §2 shipped with a ⚠ open flag on its carrier: it rode an Aries `basic-message` for **reach**, and asked whether that was the right call at all. @albertoleon7794 answered it properly — built the identical exchange **both ways** against Credo 0.6.3, measured, and retired the reach argument themselves ([`ref-06v1d-carrier`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06v1d-carrier)). This settles it as a specification change, which is what we owed them on #173.

## The carrier moves; the attachment does not

| | `0.1` | `0.2` |
|---|---|---|
| `@type` | `basic-message` (two interchangeable URIs) | `https://trusttasks.org/binding/didcomm-v1/0.2/trust-task/1.0/task` |
| Document slot | `~attach`, `@id` `trust-task` | **unchanged** |
| Human-readable line | `content` (RFC 0095) | optional advisory `comment` |

**Why the dedicated type wins**, per their measurement and recorded in §2.1:

- **It is *less* code in Credo** — ~25 lines — once `basic-message`'s content-only high-level API and its attachment-dropping message store are priced in. `0.1`'s own §2.2 documented both as costs; they were the reason.
- **It crosses a mediator identically.** v1 forwarding is type-agnostic — the type is inside the envelope.
- **It leaves the chat store alone.** `basic-message` writes every Trust Task into a wallet's conversation history, a real user-facing surface.
- **A consumer needs a handler under every option**, so reach only ever bought *visibility*, never function.

What `basic-message` genuinely retained is **visible degradation in a mixed fleet** — an unaware wallet shows a harmless "Trust Task: …" line where a dedicated type is dropped silently. §2.1 records that as an accepted loss rather than arguing it away: capability negotiation ([SPEC §11](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#11-discovery-and-capability-negotiation), RFC 0031) is what gates a peer speaking Trust Tasks, so a peer that never negotiated should not be sent one.

The attachment arguments were about the *slot*, not the carrier, so they carry over intact.

## Also in 0.2

- **The `@type` is an [RFC 0020](https://github.com/hyperledger/aries-rfcs/tree/main/concepts/0020-message-types) message type URI**, and §1 gives its decomposition so Aries tooling routes it as a protocol rather than an opaque string. Minted at `0.2` and **pinned** across later MINORs, exactly as `binding/didcomm/0.2` keeps `binding/didcomm/0.1/envelope`.
- **`0.1`'s two-interchangeable-URIs hazard is gone**, not restated — our own type has one spelling. It survives only inside §2.3, where a consumer still meets `basic-message`.
- **§2.3 requires a `0.2` consumer to accept the `0.1` carriage**, and forbids a `0.2` producer from emitting it — §5.4's receivers-first sequence. A `basic-message` carrying *no* `trust-task` attachment is explicitly **not** a Trust Task and must not be answered as one.
- **Targets framework `0.4`**, clearing the bump #208 flagged as out of scope.

## On calling this a MINOR

`0.1`'s §6 said a carriage change is breaking and requires a `MAJOR`, and in general it is right. §6.1 argues the number rather than asserting it — three reasons it is honest here:

1. **A `0.2` consumer accepts everything a `0.1` producer emits** (§2.3). That is the direction [§5.2](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#52-compatibility-rules) makes normative, satisfied in full.
2. **`0.1` anticipated this** — its §6 closed by saying a pre-adoption carriage change should be a correction to the draft rather than a new major. A new MINOR is the *more* conservative reading: it gives implementers a distinguishable URI instead of changing `0.1` under anyone who already built against it, and `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` 0.1.0 is published, so somebody could have.
3. **§5.2 permits it explicitly** while an artifact is `draft`.

And what is **not** preserved is stated plainly rather than implied: **forward compatibility**. A `0.1` consumer does not recognise a `0.2` message and drops it silently. No versioning scheme fixes that across a carriage change; deployments migrate receivers first and negotiate capability before sending.

## A registry gap found while doing this

`window.TT_BINDINGS` in `website/assets/bindings.js` is hand-edited, and `npm run build` only *copies* the bindings tree — it never enumerates it. So **`didcomm/0.2` and `didcomm-v1/0.1` were both merged, published, implemented, and completely invisible on the registry site**, for as long as nobody looked.

Same hand-maintained-list failure as the category taxonomy, so it gets the same treatment: all three missing entries added, plus **`checkBindingRegistry()`**, which fails the build on an on-disk binding with no entry or a `prosePath` that does not match its `id`, and warns on a listed binding with no directory. Verified it actually fires by removing an entry and confirming the build fails — a guard that cannot fail is worse than none. Documented in CLAUDE.md alongside the existing `data.js` callout.

No library changes: this touches no `specs/`, so no bindings regenerate and no version bumps. `npm run validate` green at 298 specs, `npm run build` clean.

## @albertoleon7794 — two things

**The `@type` value is the piece most worth your review.** I used an RFC 0020-conformant form so Credo's `parseMessageType` decomposes it into protocol `trust-task` / version `1.0` / message `task`, rather than mirroring the v2.1 binding's flat `…/envelope` URI. You have the Aries deployment experience; if Credo's routing or discover-features prefers a different shape, say so and it changes — nothing depends on it yet, which is precisely the window we spent too much of already.

**`trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` still implements the `0.1` carriage** and needs updating for this version, alongside the `thid` omit-rule from #208 you offered to send. Happy for both to come from you as one PR, or we can take it — whichever you prefer.

Refs #173.

title: v0.3.0
body:
The first tagged release since 0.2.0 (21 May). 0.2.1 was version-bumped and
written up but never tagged or published, so everything under it ships here too.

The theme is the join ceremony's asynchronous half: a community's reply now
reaches the applicant whether or not it happened to be connected when the reply
was sent, and a join left unresolved is reconciled by asking rather than by
waiting.

### Added

- **Ask a community about a join it has not answered** — every way a `Pending`
  join could previously resolve was the community volunteering something: a
  verdict, a credential, a problem-report. If any of those was lost — a socket
  down at the wrong moment, a mediator that dropped it, a decision a human took
  days later when nothing was listening — the record sat `Pending` and this
  client never asked. `join-requests/status/0.1` is the protocol's answer to
  exactly that, and OpenVTC had implemented only the receiving half
  (`handle_join_status_response` existed with nothing to trigger it).

  A minute-by-minute tick now reconciles each pollable `Pending` join, starting
  with an immediate poll at launch — a join still `Pending` when the app starts
  is precisely the one whose answer may have been lost. Per record it then backs
  off 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 minutes, capped at 15, with at most four polls per tick
  across the account (R1.4), so a parked join is noticed promptly without this
  client becoming a load source. Pacing is deliberately in memory: it is about
  this process's politeness, and a stale on-disk backoff would suppress the poll
  a fresh launch most wants to make. The poll takes the transport the submit took
  — a TSP-only community would never see a DIDComm poll.

- **Adopt the community's own request id when it first replies** — a join is
  recorded against the id of the request document *we* sent, because that is the
  only handle available until the VTC answers; the VTC mints its own and returns
  it in the first correlated reply. The submit-receipt path already swapped the
  id in, but a `refer` / `request_more` verdict carries `requestId` too and read
  straight past it — correlation there is by `thid`, so nothing needed it.

  A referred join is the one that then sits `Pending` for as long as a human
  takes, so it is the one that most needs to be askable-about later, and without
  the id there is no handle to ask with. `CommunityRecord::request_id_confirmed`
  now records *whose* id a record holds, and is the gate on polling: quoting our
  own placeholder would be asking about a request the community has never heard
  of. Records written before this default to unconfirmed, which is the safe
  reading — we cannot tell whose id they hold.

  Note what this does **not** cover: a join that received *no* reply at all has
  no confirmed id and cannot be polled. That case is not a gap here — it is
  recovered by collecting the stored mail the reply is sitting in.

### Fixed

- **Collect the messages the mediator is holding, instead of waiting to be
  pushed** — every inbound message OpenVTC has ever received arrived by live
  delivery. A mediator live-streams a message only to a recipient connected at
  the instant it lands; everything else is stored, and a stored inbox is
  redelivered **only** when a new websocket *displaces* an existing one for the
  same DID (`websocket_streaming.rs`, `if replacing`). Enabling live delivery
  drains nothing. So a listener that connects for the first time — the applicant
  persona during a join, a community's session after a restart, any identity
  whose socket was down when a reply arrived — was never told what was already
  waiting for it, and nothing in this client ever asked.

  That is the join that sits `Pending` while the community's outbox reports
  `Sent`, and it is why relaunching the app appeared to fix it: the new process's
  socket displaced the old one, and *that* is what made the mediator redelivery
  fire. The recovery was a side effect of how the previous process happened to
  exit.

  `Messaging::pickup_stored` now collects a listener's stored mail over
  message-pickup 3.0 and hands each message to the state handler on the same
  channel a live frame uses, and `pickup_on_connect` runs it on every connect —
  first connect and reconnect alike, since a reconnect is exactly when something
  may have landed with nobody attached. Messages are acknowledged **after**
  handoff, never before, the same discipline the delivery layer's own dispatcher
  follows; a frame that could not be unsealed, mapped, or queued is deliberately
  *not* acked, so nothing is deleted unread. Bounded at 200 messages per connect
  (R1.4), with the remainder logged rather than silently dropped.

  Classification is shared with the live dispatcher rather than copied
  (`classify_inbound`), so the two paths cannot drift into admitting different
  message types — and the authcrypt sender binding is applied to a collected
  message too, because these carry membership decisions and credentials and must
  not be the one path where a spoofed `from` is believed.

  Delivery is at-least-once by design (a message may also arrive live); the
  runtime loop's `SeenMessages` is what makes that harmless.

- **Start messaging before the first join, not after it** — a State-A account
  (no persona yet) ran its join with no messaging runtime at all, so the
  applicant had no socket for the entire ceremony. A community auto-admitting an
  invited join answers in under a second, so its reply was stored rather than
  streamed — and since the hot-start's listener was a *first* connect, the
  mediator never redelivered it either. The first join a new operator makes was
  the one join with no live recipient.

  The runtime now comes up **before** the State-A branch and empty
  (`start_empty_service`; `Messaging::start` runs its dispatcher before the first
  transport exists, so this is a supported state, not a stub), and the degraded
  loop hands it to `join_flow`. A State-A join therefore connects its applicant
  before submitting, exactly as the runtime-loop join already does.
  `install_listeners` then adds whatever is missing, skipping any the join
  already brought up — one websocket per DID.

  The durable join record also now states whether the applicant was connected at
  submit. A join sent from an unconnected persona is still valid, but it is the
  one that takes the collect-on-connect path, and an operator reading the log
  later could not otherwise tell that from a community that never answered.

- **Connect the applicant persona before submitting the join, not after** — a
  join over an accepted invitation is auto-admitted in well under a second, and
  the community pushes the membership credential (VMC) and role credential (VEC)
  straight back. The persona's mediator socket, though, only came up once the
  join flow had returned to the main page, so the reply arrived while its
  recipient had no live stream. A mediator live-streams a message only if the
  recipient is connected at the instant it lands: both credentials were stored
  and never pushed, and nothing polled the mailbox afterwards.

  It read as a failed join with clean logs at every hop — the community's outbox
  said *sent*, the mediator held two messages, and the membership sat `Pending`
  with no error anywhere. Observed with a ~29 s gap between the credentials
  landing and the persona's websocket registering, which is simply how long the
  operator spent on the confirmation screen.

  `run_join_sequence` now installs the persona listener as soon as the applicant
  identity exists and waits — bounded at 10 s — immediately before
  `submit_join_request`, so the socket is live for the whole window in which a
  reply can arrive and the connect is spent on the invitation resolution and VP
  build rather than on the operator's time. The wait is finite and never fatal
  (R1.2): a slow or failed connect says which it was (R6.4) and the submit goes
  out regardless — the community still admits, and the reply is collected when
  the listener does come up. `register_joined_session` already tolerated a
  listener that exists, so it now binds to it rather than installing a second.

  Cancel-safety is preserved on the pattern `minted_persona` established: the
  listener id is returned only when *this* call installed it, and is held outside
  the interruptible future so a Ctrl-C — or a failed submit — tears it down
  instead of leaving a socket open for a persona that was just rolled back. A
  reused persona already serving another community is never claimed, so its
  session survives a cancelled join.

  Independent of this, the mediator-side half of the same gap is fixed upstream
  in `affinidi-messaging-mediator` 0.18.16: enabling live delivery now redelivers
  what is already queued. Deployments want both — this change stops the reply
  from being stranded, that one stops an already-stranded reply from staying
  stranded.

### Changed

- **Refresh every dependency to its latest release** — `cargo update` across
  the whole graph, plus the manifest bumps needed to cross a major boundary:
  `vta-sdk` 0.20 → 0.21.7, `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.18 → 0.19.2,
  `trust-tasks-rs` 0.2 → 0.3.0, `trust-tasks-capability-client` 0.1 → 0.2.0,
  and the `vta-service` dev-dependency 0.13 → 0.14.16.

  One source change was needed. `affinidi-messaging-core` 0.1.6 marks
  `Protocol` `#[non_exhaustive]` and adds a `DIDCommV1` variant (Aries RFC
  0019), so the inbound dispatcher's `match` in `didcomm.rs` no longer
  compiles as written. It gained a wildcard arm that logs and drops: OpenVTC
  speaks DIDComm v2.1 and TSP, neither listener it installs ever negotiates
  v1, and nothing downstream of that match could read a v1 payload. The arm
  is also what keeps the *next* variant from being a compile break.

  Everything else rode the bump untouched — the join ceremony, the reciprocal
  VMC exchange, and the TSP leg all dispatch on `vta_sdk::protocols`
  constants rather than string literals. Verified with the full suite
  including the `#[ignore]`d e2e tests, which are the ones that actually
  exercise these crates: the in-process mediator transport round-trip, the
  join/self-remove lifecycle, and the MockVta bootstrap against
  `vta-service` 0.14.

  Two pins survive re-evaluation and stay: `rand` 0.8 and `x25519-dalek` 2.x
  are both still forced by `pgp` 0.20.0, which remains the latest release and
  declares `rand ^0.8.6` / `x25519-dalek ^2.0.1`.

  Known duplicate, upstream to fix: `did-git-sign` 0.4.1 still depends on
  `vta-sdk` 0.19.28, so the binary links two vta-sdk majors. That belongs to
  `verifiable-git-infrastructure`, not here.

- **Drop two resolved advisory ignores from `deny.toml`** — RUSTSEC-2026-0215
  (`smallstr` unmaintained) and RUSTSEC-2024-0370 (`proc-macro-error`
  unmaintained). Both crates left the dependency graph with this refresh,
  exactly as each ignore's comment predicted, and `cargo deny` now reports
  them as unmatched. The remaining ignores still match and stay.

- **Follow the VTC Trust Tasks onto the `spec/vtc` registry authority** —
  `vta-sdk` 0.20.0 → 0.20.1 (and `trust-tasks-rs` 0.2.26 → 0.2.38). The VTC's
  Trust Tasks have moved off the non-conformant
  `trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/…` authority to the canonical registry at
  `trusttasks.org/spec/vtc/…`
  (OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#806, dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#144).

  No source change was needed: the join ceremony and the reciprocal-VMC
  exchange dispatch on `vta_sdk::protocols` constants rather than string
  literals, so the new URIs arrive with the bump —
  `MEMBER_REQUEST_VMC_TYPE` and `MEMBER_VMC_TYPE` now read
  `spec/vtc/members/{request-vmc,vmc}/0.1`, and the join-request and
  self-remove receipts likewise. That indirection is why this is a lockfile
  change and not an audit of every dispatch site.

  The inbound router already accepted both authorities — `OPENVTC_CATCH_ALL_PATTERN`
  gained its `spec/vtc/` arm ahead of the migration precisely so migrated
  traffic would not be dropped before dispatch. It stays dual-arm for now:
  the `openvtc/vtc/` arm can be retired once no supported VTC emits it, and
  eight VTC tasks are still on the old authority awaiting a canonical fold.

body:
chore(release): 0.3.0

First tagged release since 0.2.0 (21 May). 0.2.1 was version-bumped and
written up in the changelog but never tagged or published, so everything
under it ships here too — this is the first artifact to carry it.

Minor, not patch: #219 adds an outbound protocol verb

runtime behaviour materially — every listener connect now collects the
mail the mediator was holding. Pre-1.0 that is a minor bump.

true`), so `[workspace.package] version` is the only place it is written
— except that `openvtc-core`'s own path-dependency requirement has to
move with it. Left at `"0.2"` the workspace stops resolving outright:

(`CommunityRecord::request_id_confirmed`) is `#[serde(default)]`, so an
existing config loads unchanged and reads as "we hold our own request
id", which is the safe interpretation.

title: fix(ts-bindings): identify a schema's root type by title, not by position (#215)
body:
fix(ts-bindings): identify a schema's root type by title, not by position (#215)

`Payload` aliased the wrong type in the TypeScript bindings for 14 published
specifications. `rootTypeName()` took the first `export interface|type` in the
compiled output, on the assumption that the root always comes first. It does
not: where a schema `$ref`s a shared definition, json-schema-to-typescript may
hoist that definition to its own exported type ahead of the root, and the
first-match rule then picked it up.

So chat/message/0.1, trust-ceremony-receipt/0.1, consent/request/1.0, both
audit/* and all three task-consent/* specs — and vrc/relationships/issue/0.1 and
witness/session/submit/0.1, published yesterday in #213 — each exported

    export type Payload = DigestMultibase;   // = string

in place of their request payload interface.

Nothing downstream could catch it. The drift check compares the generator's
output to itself, so a consistently wrong alias is consistently wrong. `tsc` is
satisfied because the alias is well-formed. No test asserts what `Payload`
resolves to. This is the same failure mode as the response-type drop fixed in
#174, and it survived because the rule that had to be right was a positional
guess.

The root is now identified by the name the compiler derives from the schema's
own `title` — the same derivation json-schema-to-typescript uses — and only
where that name is actually present in the emitted output; position remains the
fallback for a schema with no usable title.

A positional guess replaced by a better guess is still a guess, so the fix
carries an invariant: an object-rooted schema whose root resolves to a *bare*
alias (`= string`, `= DigestMultibase`) now fails the build, since that is the
shape this failure always takes. Scoped to bare aliases deliberately — an object
type literal or a union is a legitimate root form, and an earlier draft of the
check rejected auth/revoke-session, credential-exchange/issue and keys/import
for compiling to `export type X = { … }`.

Not a breaking change: the old alias was unusable. Assigning a real payload to a
`string` does not compile, so no correct consumer could have depended on it.
The Rust bindings were never affected — trust-tasks-rs is unchanged in content
at 0.6.4 and moves only to keep the two libraries in step.

Refs #173.

title: feat(vtc): converge the VRC digest onto DigestMultibase (relationships 0.2)
body:
One of the two items I listed as still open on our side in #173. `vtc/relationships/request`, `publish` and `list` carried the credential digest as **`vrcSha256`** — a bare lowercase-hex SHA-256 — while #213 published `vrc/relationships/*` on the framework's `DigestMultibase`. Two relationship families disagreeing about how to name the same kind of value.

## Why the old form is wrong

The framework's shared `DigestMultibase` definition names all three defects in its own description:

- **A bare hex string hard-codes one algorithm into the wire contract.** Moving off SHA-256 later needs a schema revision rather than a different multihash prefix.
- **It names no base encoding**, leaving a verifier to infer base16 from context.
- **`0.1` named no canonicalization.** This is the one that actually bites. "SHA-256 of the VRC" is not reproducible for a JSON document, so two conforming implementations can compute different values for the same credential and neither is wrong — and `request`'s own description *promises* its digest "matches the digest `vtc/relationships/publish` reports once the credential is lodged", with `list` repeating it per entry. All three are meant to be the same value, which they cannot reliably be without a stated canonicalization.

## What changed

`0.2` of each carries **`vrcDigestMultibase`**, `$ref`'ing `_framework/0.3#/$defs/DigestMultibase`, over the **RFC 8785 (JCS)** canonicalization, now stated. Required-ness is unchanged per spec (optional on `request`'s response, required on `publish`'s response and on each `list` entry). All three also move to `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.4"`.

The three move together because their digests are the same value by design; converging one without the others would break the tie the descriptions promise.

## Versioning

Breaking on the wire, released as a **`MINOR` increment** under [§5.2](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#52-compatibility-rules)'s `draft` allowance. §5.2's in-place errata rule explicitly does *not* apply — it covers `$ref` re-pins "where the re-pin does not change the payload's effective wire shape", and hex → multibase changes it.

`0.1` remains published and unchanged. Each `0.2` carries a **Changes from 0.1** section with the §5.4 expand-then-contract sequence, and a point worth stating explicitly: a `0.2` consumer **MUST** still accept `0.1` documents, which carry `vrcSha256` — a member `0.2`'s schema rejects. The two are distinguished by the *Type URI*'s version, not by sniffing the payload.

Libraries bumped **0.6.2 → 0.6.3** — additive, since `0.1` remains generated alongside. `npm run validate` green at **298 specs**, both drift checks clean, `cargo test --features validate`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo fmt` and the TS suite green.

## Deliberately not in scope

`provision/integration/{0.1,0.2}` (`digest`) and `vault/_shared/{0.1,0.2}` (`sha256`) also carry bare-hex digests. They are over **opaque bytes** rather than JSON, so the canonicalization defect does not apply and only the encoding argument does — and `vault/_shared` is a shared component, so re-pinning it forces a new version of every consuming spec under §5.4's coupling rule. Worth doing, but as its own decision rather than swept in here.

## Also found, not fixed here

While regenerating: the TypeScript generator emits **`export type Payload = DigestMultibase`** for every spec that `$ref`s a shared definition which hoists ahead of the root type — `rootTypeName()` in `scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs` takes the first `export interface|type` in the compiled output. **14 already-published specs are affected**, including two that shipped in #213. The Rust generator is unaffected. Raising separately, because the fix changes compile-visible types across all of them and needs its own version decision.

Refs #173. Follows #213.

title: feat(join): ask a community about a join it has not answered
body:
feat(join): ask a community about a join it has not answered

Every way a Pending join could resolve was the community volunteering
something: a verdict, a credential, a problem-report. Lose any of those —
a socket down at the wrong moment, a mediator that dropped it, a decision
a human took days later when nothing was listening — and the record sits
Pending while this client never asks. `join-requests/status/0.1` is the
protocol's answer to exactly that, and OpenVTC had implemented only the
receiving half: `handle_join_status_response` existed with nothing to
trigger it.

A 60s tick now reconciles each pollable Pending join, first poll
immediate — a join still Pending at launch is precisely the one whose
answer may have been lost — then per-record backoff 1/2/4/8 minutes
capped at 15, at most four polls per tick across the account (R1.4).
Pacing is in memory on purpose: it is about this process's politeness,
and a stale on-disk backoff would suppress the poll a fresh launch most
wants to make. The poll takes the transport the submit took, since a
TSP-only community would never see a DIDComm poll. Spawned detached
rather than through background_dispatch: there is no outcome to apply on
the loop thread (the reply arrives on the persona's listener and goes
through inbound dispatch like anything else), and the pacer prevents
pile-up by marking a record polled before the send.

The gate this needed did not exist. A join is recorded against the id of
the document WE sent — the only handle available until the VTC answers —
while the VTC mints its own (`join/mod.rs`: `id: Uuid::new_v4()`) and
returns it in the first correlated reply. The submit-receipt path already
swapped it in, but a refer/request_more verdict carries `requestId` too
and read straight past it, because correlation there is by `thid` and
nothing needed the id. A referred join is the one that then sits Pending
for as long as a human takes — the one that most needs to be
askable-about — so it is now adopted from whichever reply lands first.
`CommunityRecord::request_id_confirmed` records whose id a record holds
and gates the poll: quoting our own placeholder is asking about a request
the community has never heard of, and is answered as such. Pre-existing
records default to unconfirmed, which is the safe reading.

Scope, stated plainly: a join that received NO reply has no confirmed id
and cannot be polled. That is not a gap this can close — the id does not
exist on our side — and it is not the case for it either; that one is
recovered by collecting the stored mail its reply is sitting in.

`build_trust_task_document` is generalised out of the submit builder
rather than copied, so both verbs produce the envelope the VTC dispatches
on (a bare payload is `malformedRequest`, "missing field `id`" — how the
submit failed before #138).

  cargo test --workspace                       → 677 passed, 0 failed
  cargo test --workspace -- --include-ignored  → 690 passed, 0 failed
  cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings    → clean
  cargo fmt --all                              → clean

No e2e: the round trip needs a VTC to answer, and vtc-service is not in
this workspace's test graph (vta-service is). What is covered here is
everything on this side of the wire — the document shape, the id
adoption on both reply paths, the pollable gate, and the pacer.

title: fix(messaging): collect stored mail on connect, and start messaging before the first join
body:
fix(messaging): collect stored mail on connect, and start messaging before the first join

Every inbound message this client has ever received arrived by live
delivery. A mediator live-streams a message only to a recipient connected
at the instant it lands; everything else is stored — and a stored inbox is
redelivered ONLY when a new websocket displaces an existing one for the
same DID (`websocket_streaming.rs`, `if replacing`). Enabling live
delivery drains nothing. So a listener connecting for the first time was
never told what was already waiting for it, and nothing here ever asked.

That is the join that sits Pending while the community's outbox reports
Sent. It is also why relaunching "fixed" it: the new process's socket
displaced the old one, and that is what made the mediator redelivery fire.
The recovery was a side effect of how the previous process happened to
exit — #217 closed the window for the runtime-loop join, but left every
residual case depending on that accident.

`Messaging::pickup_stored` collects a listener's stored mail over
message-pickup 3.0 and hands each message to the state handler on the same
channel a live frame uses; `pickup_on_connect` runs it on every connect,
first and subsequent alike, since a reconnect is exactly when something
may have landed with nobody attached. Ack is after handoff, never before —
the delivery layer's own discipline — and a frame that could not be
unsealed, mapped or queued is deliberately NOT acked, so nothing is
deleted unread; that also terminates the drain, since an unacked frame at
the head of the queue would otherwise be refetched forever. Bounded at 200
per connect (R1.4) with the remainder logged, not silently dropped.

Classification is shared with the live dispatcher (`classify_inbound`)
rather than copied, so the two paths cannot drift into admitting different
types, and the authcrypt sender binding is applied to a collected message
too: these carry membership decisions and credentials and must not be the
one path where a spoofed `from` is believed.

Second half: a State-A account ran its join with no messaging runtime at
all (`join_flow(.., None)`), so the applicant had no socket for the whole
ceremony — and the hot-start's listener was a *first* connect, which the
mediator does not redeliver to. The first join a new operator makes was
the one join with no live recipient. The runtime now starts before the
State-A branch and empty (`start_empty_service`), the degraded loop hands
it to `join_flow`, and `install_listeners` adds what is missing afterwards
without duplicating the socket the join already opened. The removed
"DIDComm service failed to start" fallback was unreachable: `start_service`
never returned `Err`.

The durable join record now also states whether the applicant was
connected at submit — a join sent offline is valid but takes the
collect-on-connect path, which the log could not previously distinguish
from a community that never answered.

  cargo test --workspace                       → 666 passed, 0 failed
  cargo test --workspace -- --include-ignored  → 680 passed, 0 failed
  cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings    → clean
  cargo fmt --all                              → clean

The new e2e (`a_message_stored_before_the_listener_existed_is_collected_on_connect`)
was verified to fail with the pickup disabled: the message is stored, bob
connects, enables live delivery, and hears nothing. Its first draft passed
without the fix because the send and the connect were milliseconds apart —

title: fix(messaging): collect stored mail on connect, and start messaging before the first join (#218)
body:
fix(messaging): collect stored mail on connect, and start messaging before the first join (#218)

* fix(messaging): collect stored mail on connect, and start messaging before the first join

Every inbound message this client has ever received arrived by live
delivery. A mediator live-streams a message only to a recipient connected
at the instant it lands; everything else is stored — and a stored inbox is
redelivered ONLY when a new websocket displaces an existing one for the
same DID (`websocket_streaming.rs`, `if replacing`). Enabling live
delivery drains nothing. So a listener connecting for the first time was
never told what was already waiting for it, and nothing here ever asked.

That is the join that sits Pending while the community's outbox reports
Sent. It is also why relaunching "fixed" it: the new process's socket
displaced the old one, and that is what made the mediator redelivery fire.
The recovery was a side effect of how the previous process happened to
exit — #217 closed the window for the runtime-loop join, but left every
residual case depending on that accident.

`Messaging::pickup_stored` collects a listener's stored mail over
message-pickup 3.0 and hands each message to the state handler on the same
channel a live frame uses; `pickup_on_connect` runs it on every connect,
first and subsequent alike, since a reconnect is exactly when something
may have landed with nobody attached. Ack is after handoff, never before —
the delivery layer's own discipline — and a frame that could not be
unsealed, mapped or queued is deliberately NOT acked, so nothing is
deleted unread; that also terminates the drain, since an unacked frame at
the head of the queue would otherwise be refetched forever. Bounded at 200
per connect (R1.4) with the remainder logged, not silently dropped.

Classification is shared with the live dispatcher (`classify_inbound`)
rather than copied, so the two paths cannot drift into admitting different
types, and the authcrypt sender binding is applied to a collected message
too: these carry membership decisions and credentials and must not be the
one path where a spoofed `from` is believed.

Second half: a State-A account ran its join with no messaging runtime at
all (`join_flow(.., None)`), so the applicant had no socket for the whole
ceremony — and the hot-start's listener was a *first* connect, which the
mediator does not redeliver to. The first join a new operator makes was
the one join with no live recipient. The runtime now starts before the
State-A branch and empty (`start_empty_service`), the degraded loop hands
it to `join_flow`, and `install_listeners` adds what is missing afterwards
without duplicating the socket the join already opened. The removed
"DIDComm service failed to start" fallback was unreachable: `start_service`
never returned `Err`.

The durable join record now also states whether the applicant was
connected at submit — a join sent offline is valid but takes the
collect-on-connect path, which the log could not previously distinguish
from a community that never answered.

  cargo test --workspace                       → 666 passed, 0 failed
  cargo test --workspace -- --include-ignored  → 680 passed, 0 failed
  cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings    → clean
  cargo fmt --all                              → clean

The new e2e (`a_message_stored_before_the_listener_existed_is_collected_on_connect`)
was verified to fail with the pickup disabled: the message is stored, bob
connects, enables live delivery, and hears nothing. Its first draft passed
without the fix because the send and the connect were milliseconds apart —
the frame was still in flight — so it now waits out a real offline window
before connecting the recipient.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(docs): don't link a private const from public documentation

 runs with `-D warnings` in CI, and
`rustdoc::private_intra_doc_links` rejects an intra-doc link from
`pickup_stored`'s public documentation to `PICKUP_MAX`, which is a
private policy constant. The bound is still named — it is what an
operator would grep for — just not linked.

  RUSTDOCFLAGS='-D warnings' cargo doc --workspace --no-deps  → clean

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(specs): the witnessed relationship exchange — vrc/* and witness/* (draft 0.1)
body:
The relationship-witnessing worked example invited in #173 — four draft specifications expressing the peer-to-peer witnessed relationship exchange that DTG Core Credentials' `taskContext` binding depends on. This is the test of whether the qualifying profile is satisfiable by a real specification, answered in the affirmative — with running code behind every design decision.

## The four specifications

| Spec | Role | Qualifying-profile relevance |
|---|---|---|
| `vrc/relationship/propose` | Opens the **mutual** peer-to-peer relationship exchange; pairwise relationship DIDs exchanged | Proof OPTIONAL both variants — in-exchange documents under authcrypt (§4.7.1) |
| `vrc/relationship/issue` | Delivers one party's signed VRC; performed once each direction; DTG delivery idiom (receipt, no echo — per the `vmc`/`join-requests/accept` guidance in #173) | Proof REQUIRED on the request (retained credential delivery) |
| `witness/session` | Opens the witness ceremony **as its own exchange**, nested via `parentThreadId` (§4.9.2); its `#response` issues the session challenge | Proof REQUIRED on the response; **this document's `id` is what a VWC's `taskContext` carries** (§4.9.1 innermost-exchange anchoring) |
| `witness/session/submit` | Presentation bound to the challenge; the **mandatory** `#response` delivers the VWC | Proof REQUIRED both variants; the response **is the outcome evidence** a VWC presentation must ship |

The peer-to-peer family is deliberately distinct from `vtc/relationships/*` (community-mediated, one-directional): this exchange is mutual and optionally witnessed, which that family cannot express — the "shape it cannot express" signal asked for in #173.

## Authored from a running exchange

Every structural decision executes before it is asserted: [`tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange) runs the full shape between three Credo 0.6.3 agents with the `@openvtc/trust-tasks` pipeline on every receive — the two threads, the `parentThreadId` nesting, the `taskContext` anchoring, `proofRequired` enforced on an unproofed witness response, and the retained `submit#response` (2,213 bytes) passing a third-party pairing check. A compatibility rung ([`ref-06w2-compat`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06w2-compat)) additionally proves, against the production witness implementation's own compiled functions, that these documents and the legacy protocol produce byte-identical witness credentials — the recast changes the wire clothes, not the ceremony.

## Registry housekeeping (per CLAUDE.md)

`npm run validate` green (294 specs); TS + Rust bindings regenerated, both drift checks clean; `cargo test` and the TS suite green; `trust-tasks-rs` and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` bumped 0.6.0 → 0.6.1 (additive) with a changelog entry — **note: merging releases 0.6.1 via `publish.yml`**. Review history: Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#3.

## Design notes

The `vwc` and `vrc` payloads are deliberately opaque objects — their schemas belong to DTG Core Credentials, and the layering rule (a task specification does not define credential schemas) is stated in each spec. `witness/session` isolates its binding material (`{challenge, domain}`) in one place, so a future canonical-transcript upgrade replaces a member rather than the ceremony. Known follow-up specifications for the family: `witness/announce` (the capability broadcast, the one bearer task) and `witness/reporting-did/register`.

## Three decisions to settle in review

1. **Namespace**: top-level `vrc/` and `witness/` slugs are proposed (category: `credentials`); CODEOWNERS entries deliberately await the slug decision.
2. **Bilateral submission**: the ceremony is bilateral in practice — both parties submit under one challenge and each receives a VWC; today's implementation runs exactly one shared session both parties join. Whether the session response should enumerate expected submitters connects to the ceremony layer's `perRole` multiplicity.
3. **Delivery vs evidence**: today's implementation delivers the VWC over a separate credential-exchange flow after the session. The alternative: keep delivery on that channel and have `submit#response` carry a **reference + digest** rather than the full credential — the response stays the proof-bearing outcome evidence while shrinking retained evidence and separating "credential delivery" from "completion evidence". This changes the `submit#response` payload schema, so it is cheaper settled here than after adoption.

title: feat(specs): the witnessed relationship exchange — vrc/relationships/* and witness/* (draft 0.1)
body:
The relationship-witnessing worked example invited in #173, **taken over from #209** with the review findings applied. Four draft specifications for the peer-to-peer witnessed relationship exchange that DTG Core Credentials' `taskContext` binding depends on — and the test of whether the qualifying profile is satisfiable by a real specification, answered in the affirmative.

Authored by @albertoleon7794 in #209, against a running three-agent exchange ([`ref-06w-witnessed-exchange`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange)). This PR exists rather than a review on #209 because that branch lives in an org-owned fork, which GitHub's maintainer-edit grant cannot reach, and the version bump had collided with a 0.6.1 already released from `main`.

| Spec | Role |
|---|---|
| `vrc/relationships/propose` | Opens the mutual exchange; pairwise relationship DIDs, and whether it will be witnessed |
| `vrc/relationships/issue` | Delivers one party's signed VRC, with a receipt naming what was stored. Once in each direction |
| `witness/session` | Opens **one party's** session with a witness; its `id` is what that party's VWC carries as `taskContext` |
| `witness/session/submit` | The presentation bound to the challenge; the mandatory `#response` is the outcome evidence |

## What changed from #209

**Mechanical**

- Slug `vrc/relationship/*` → **`vrc/relationships/*`**, for consistency with the community-mediated `vtc/relationships/*` it sits beside. (Answers open question 1; `witness/` stays top-level — `webvh/witness/publish` is a different concept already namespaced under its own domain.)
- **Two broken SPEC.md anchors.** Both witness specs linked `#491-citing-an-exchange-as-evidence`; the §4.9.1 heading is *Naming an exchange from outside the framework*. These were the load-bearing citations of the whole set.
- Rebased past the **0.6.1 collision** — `main` had already published 0.6.1 for both libraries. Now 0.6.2.

**Substantive**

- **The digest was hand-rolled.** `vrcDigestMultibase` inlined `^z[1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z]+$` and described it as the registry's converged digest form. The registry *has* that form — `_framework/0.3#/$defs/DigestMultibase`, already `$ref`'d by twelve files — and the copy dropped the base64url branch [W3C CID 1.0 §2.4](https://www.w3.org/TR/cid-1.0/) normatively requires along with the `minLength` floor, so `"z1"` validated. Now `$ref`'d.

- **The delivery receipt named nothing.** It was `received: const true` plus an *optional* digest. Both directions of the exchange share one `threadId`, and a `#response` carries no `inResponseTo` — §8.2 added that to the *error* response only — so nothing told a party which of its two deliveries a receipt answered. The digest is now **REQUIRED** and **computed by the receiver over the credential as stored**, which both names the artifact (the `vmc` / `join-requests/accept` idiom stormer78 pointed at in #173) and supplies the correlation. A separate thread per direction was the alternative; it would make one mutual exchange look like two to every consumer that groups by thread.

- **The second party had no way into the session.** The session was described as shared, but the challenge travels in a `#response`, which reaches only the party that sent the request. A session is now explicitly **bilateral** — each party opens its own with the same witness, both naming the same `parties` pair, each with its own challenge and its own `taskContext` anchor. This is the framework's own model (a Trust Task is bilateral, §2), it keeps `taskContext` a document `id` exactly as #179 and cred-spec #18 expect, and distinct challenges stop either party's presentation satisfying the other's session. *This is the change most worth checking against the reference run* — see below.

- **`witnessed: true` had no acceptance channel.** The proposal asked; nothing answered, yet the `issue` leg required the witnessing to complete first. The response now answers it, and silence resolves to **unwitnessed** — the failure mode of under-claiming is a party who asks again, of over-claiming a relationship recorded as witnessed that nobody witnessed.

- **"Ceremony" collided with framework 0.4.** The specs target 0.4, which reserves *Trust Ceremony* for a flow of several tasks (§4.11, `/ceremony/` subtree). The prose used it for a single two-document exchange. It now says *session* or *witnessing*. §4.11.1 forbids a specification from declaring anything about ceremonies, so composing the two sessions into an enactment remains available and needs no change here — noted non-normatively in `witness/session`.

- **`submit#response`: full VWC, plus a digest.** Answering open question 3. It carries the credential because the response is *mandatory* where a second delivery flow would not be — a witness that has verified the presentation has everything it needs to issue, and a further exchange adds a failure mode (session succeeded, credential never arrived). The REQUIRED digest means the binding a reference-and-digest design would give is available anyway, and a later version can drop `vwc` to a reference without changing how a verifier pairs the two.

- `exposure.discloses: none` on the `issue` leg now carries its rationale, since the §7.3 item 13/14 proof floors key off it.

**Deliberately not changed:** `vrc` and `vwc` stay unconstrained `type: object` with prose. That is the house pattern — `vtc/relationships/request` types its VRC identically — and the layering rule (a task specification does not define credential schemas) is right. Worth knowing that it means `{"vwc": {}}` validates.

## Housekeeping

CODEOWNERS entries for both new namespaces. Bindings regenerated — `npm run validate` green at **295 specs**, both drift checks clean, `cargo test --features validate`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo fmt` and the TS suite (43 tests) green. Libraries bumped **0.6.1 → 0.6.2** with a changelog entry, so **merging releases 0.6.2** via `publish.yml`.

## @albertoleon7794 — three things to check against your reference runs

1. **The bilateral session** is the one that could contradict your implementation, which runs one shared session both parties join. If a shared session is load-bearing for something I have not seen — a transcript, a joint attestation, the `perRole` multiplicity you mentioned — say so and we will revisit; the framework-native alternative is composing the two sessions as one *Trust Ceremony* enactment, which §4.11 now supports without changing these specs.
2. **The receiver-computed digest** adds a canonicalization step to the receiving party that the copied-value design did not have.
3. **`witnessed` on the response** is a new member your implementation will not be setting yet.

Also flagged for a later PR, out of scope here: `vtc/relationships/request/0.1` carries `vrcSha256` as a bare hex digest, which `DigestMultibase`'s own description calls non-conforming. These specs are on the converged form; that one still needs bringing across.

Refs #173. Supersedes #209.

title: fix(bindings): reconcile the didcomm-v1 omit-rule with §4, and aim it at the party who can act
body:
Review follow-ups on #208. The omit-never-rewrite disposition is right and the Credo evidence behind it is solid — these are the edges around it, found while reviewing that PR against the framework and RFC 0008/0095.

Attempted as a push to #208's branch first; the fork is org-owned, and GitHub's maintainer-edit grant only reaches forks in personal accounts. Hence a follow-up rather than an amendment in place.

### The two that matter

**§4 contradicted the new rule.** The error-mapping section closed with an instruction to return the error response "with `~thread.thid` continuing the exchange" — which the omit rule makes impossible for precisely the exchanges that trigger it. It now defers to §3.1 and points at `inResponseTo` ([SPEC §8.2](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#82-error-payload)), which names the reported-on document directly and does not need the transport to carry a thread at all. That mechanism landed in 0.3 for a closely related reason, and it is the right answer here.

**Omitting the field is not neutral.** RFC 0008 *defaults* an absent `thid` to the message `@id` — a fact §3.1 already relies on for the consumer comparison rule. So an omission does not leave the message unthreaded; it puts each message of the exchange in a v1 thread of its own, named by a value the transport minted. Nothing the framework relies on is lost, but transport-level correlation is, and tooling that groups by `~thread` will not group it. A new paragraph says so and forbids inferring continuation from a defaulted `thid`.

### The rest

- **The conformant-id `SHOULD` was addressed to nobody in particular.** The case that actually forces an omission is a *responder* whose `threadId` was inherited from a document another party minted, possibly on another transport — it cannot repair that value. Initiation is the only point in an exchange where the choice is free, and §4.9 already permits minting there, so the `SHOULD` now names the initiator. Extended explicitly to the document's `id` (§4.9's fallback `thid`) and to `parentThreadId`.
- **The shape excludes more than colons.** The prose motivated the rule entirely via `urn:uuid:`; it also rejects any value under eight characters, and base64's `+` and `=`. Named, so an implementer testing only the URN form is not surprised twice.
- **`sent_time` is not a decorator.** RFC 0095 defines it as a top-level member of the message, alongside `content`. It no longer sits inside the decorator-tolerance rule, which mis-described what it governs.
- **Placement.** The representability block had been inserted between the **Producers** rule and that rule's own rationale paragraph, so the rationale read as a continuation of the new material. Moved below it.
- **`authors:`** gains the binding's co-author, per the takeover agreed in #173.

No wire-format or normative-disposition change beyond the two reconciliations above; `draft` status and `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.3"` are untouched. `npm run validate` green (291 specs; the `vta/did-templates` and fenced-JSON warnings are pre-existing on `main`).

/cc @albertoleon7794 — flagging in particular the `inResponseTo` fallback in §4, since it bears on the v1 binding draft you are taking over, and the initiator-side minting rule, which is the one that changes what an implementation has to do.

Refs #173, #208.
